title: Publishing Under AI (2025–2026)
position_scale: -2 argues for pole_a (the more cautious side: keep or tighten human control); +2 argues for pole_b (lets AI in or opens up the system); ±1 leans that way or mainly supplies evidence for it; 0 addresses the question without taking a side.

stages.label: Drafting & Framing
stages.hook: Fluency stops signaling effort; prose-thinking meets executable workflows.

stages.label: Citations & Synthesis
stages.hook: Phantom DOIs and shallow secondary loops enter submitted bibliographies.

stages.label: Submission & Triage
stages.hook: Zero-cost submissions strain editors; disclosure mandates decouple from practice.

shockwaves.headline: Distinct estimators put AI-assisted writing at ≥13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts and 89% of December 2025 PMC full texts
shockwaves.detail: Excess-vocabulary tracking across 15M+ PubMed abstracts placed 2024 LLM-assisted prevalence at ≥13.5%, while a newer estimator applied to structured English-language PubMed Central full texts estimates 89% in December 2025 (and 68% in Discussion versus 32% in Methods on random 255-word crops). Because the corpora, text units, and statistical estimators differ, the two figures measure distinct slices of biomedical writing.

shockwaves.headline: Prose complexity flips its observational association with review outcomes; separately, LLM rewrites compress stylistic variance
shockwaves.detail: Across 2.1M preprints and 28K peer reviews, linguistic complexity showed opposite observational associations with later peer-reviewed publication and review scores in manuscripts classified as LLM-assisted versus undetected papers, while Renault et al. showed that first-detection adoption dating can mechanically inflate apparent productivity jumps. Separately, controlled rewrites of 1,000 arXiv abstracts and 1,000 Reddit stories narrowed writing-complexity variance across most tested models and prompts.

shockwaves.headline: Papers with at least one possibly fabricated reference climb from 6.3 to 23.0 per 10,000 (2023–Q1 2026)
shockwaves.detail: Screening 500,000 peer-reviewed papers in chemistry, physics, materials science, engineering and computer science found papers with at least one possibly fabricated reference rising from 6.3 per 10,000 in 2023 to 23.0 per 10,000 in the first quarter of 2026 (85.8% precision on masked checks; ‘fabricated’ means the reference could not be verified). The same team's audit of 2.5 million biomedical papers in PubMed Central found 4,046 fabricated references in 2,810 papers, at a rate that rose more than twelvefold to about 57 per 10,000 papers by early 2026, and an audit of 111 million references across arXiv, bioRxiv, SSRN and PubMed Central conservatively estimates 146,932 hallucinated citations in 2025 alone. At NeurIPS and USENIX Security 2025, about 1 in 20 accepted papers carried at least two suspect references before human checking, and most flags checked by hand proved recoverable or false. A Nature correspondence argues that confirmed hallucinated citations should count as misconduct.

shockwaves.headline: Public AI disclosures appear in ~0.1% of sampled papers and private ones in 3–6% of medical-journal submissions, while arXiv and AJPS cap submissions
shockwaves.detail: Across 5,114 journals and 5.2 million papers, He and Bu found that about 70% of sampled Q1 journals had AI policies by January 2025, yet public writing-assistance statements appeared in only 76 of 75,172 sampled full texts published since 2023 (about 0.1%); a PNAS exchange debated how far private submission declarations change that picture. Private declarations at two medical publishers tell a similar story: 5.7% of 25,114 research manuscripts submitted to BMJ Group journals in 2024 and 3.3% of 105,538 manuscripts submitted to 13 JAMA Network journals (rising to about 6% by October 2025) disclosed AI use, far below the 28–76% of researchers who report using it in surveys. In autumn 2026, JACC reaffirmed its exemption for writing-only help, arXiv capped submitters at two papers per calendar month (a year after its computer-science section began requiring peer review for review and position papers), AJPS limited authors to three submissions in any rolling 12 months, and bioRxiv and medRxiv reserved the right to rate-limit authors.

shockwaves.headline: Detected paper-mill output grows rapidly while PhD-level readers reach 50.5% accuracy telling authentic from selected AI-manipulated figures
shockwaves.detail: Forensic network analysis finds suspected paper-mill output growing far faster than publications overall, and a classifier trained on retracted mill papers flags 9.87% of 2.6 million cancer-research papers as similar to mill output, a share that rose from about 1% of annual output in the early 2000s to more than 15% by the early 2020s, including in the top 10% of journals. Commentators warn that agentic AI now mines open cohorts such as NHANES and UK Biobank at speed. In a controlled study, 24 PhD-level biomedical readers judging authentic and selected AI-manipulated Western blot and tumour images were right 50.5% of the time on average.

shockwaves.headline: Classifiers flag 12–21% of reviews as AI-written, and ICML catches 1% of reviews breaking a no-LLM pledge
shockwaves.detail: One preprint classifier flags about 20% of sampled ICLR 2025 reviews and 12% of sampled 2025 Nature Communications reviews as AI-generated, and a detector vendor reports 21% of ICLR 2026 reviews as fully AI-generated. At ICML 2026, hidden watermark phrases caught 795 reviews (about 1%) by reviewers who had agreed not to use LLMs, and in an anonymous survey 22.5% of reviewers under the no-LLM policy said they had used one anyway. An editorial sets a Frontiers survey, in which 53% of reviewers reported using AI, beside an informal count at one journal where more than 95% declared non-use. Controlled experiments show AI reviews agreeing excessively with one another and AI scores rising after an LLM rewrites a paper, and detectors misfire: Pangram and GPTZero label 3.1% and 3.4% of human-written, AI-polished reviews as fully AI-generated.

shockwaves.signal_type: Adversarial fragility vs. bounded technical screening
shockwaves.headline: AI reviewers catch planted errors and win editors' blinded preference tests, yet a hidden sentence can flip their verdicts
shockwaves.detail: In a clinical-trial preprint, 15 LLMs scored 53–96% on detecting major errors planted in three historical trial reports, against a 27% mean among journal peer reviewers in the original study, and 58–99% on recent trials (the top three models on three of 58), scored by LLM judges without new human comparators; models also flagged 14–29% of error categories in unmodified reports. At AAAI-26, all 22,977 papers that reached full review received an AI review, which surveyed authors and committee members preferred on six of nine criteria while finding it more prone to dwell on minor issues. In a social-science working paper, three former editors preferred AI reviews in 26 of 30 blinded judgments without reading the manuscripts. AI reviewers are also easy to steer: a hidden nudge flipped the accept-or-reject recommendations of four commercial models on medical manuscripts in 84% of cases, and warning them barely helped. A randomized ICLR trial tests a narrower role, feedback on human reviews.

shockwaves.signal_type: Autonomous pipelines, workflow blind spots & executable packages
shockwaves.headline: AI Scientist enters Nature, ALIFE 2026 accepts a co-created paper, and PNAS shows why manuscript-only audits miss flaws
shockwaves.detail: Alongside Nature's report on The AI Scientist (covering a human-filtered, protocol-withdrawn workshop run) and the reported acceptance at ALIFE 2026 of an Error Diffusion paper that human researchers produced using a development version of The Agentic Scientist, a 2026 PNAS study showed that giving an LLM-based auditor agent logs and code lifted its accuracy from 53.7% to 81.5% on a constructed flaw benchmark — complementing PaperBench's partial-credit rubric scores (21.0% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet with BasicAgent; 24.4–26.0% for o1 with IterativeAgent; not the share of papers replicated), ClaimNov's controlled novelty benchmark, and Paper2Agent's 74/100 MCP conversions.

fault_lines.question: When fluent scientific prose costs almost nothing to generate, does writing a manuscript still test scientific thinking, or has prose become a secondary view layer over data and code?

pole_a.label: Writing IS the thinking
pole_a.summary: Drafting prose forces authors to discover gaps in logic and own every claim; delegating text generation produces smooth paragraphs around half-formed ideas and shifts cognitive effort onto readers.

pole_b.label: Executable package first
pole_b.summary: The 5,000-word static essay compresses messy computation into narrative theatre; verified datasets, runnable code, and machine-checkable claims should be the primary record, with prose rendered per reader.

fault_lines.hinge: Whether scientific reasoning happens during prose composition itself or upstream in experimental design and formal analysis.

fault_lines.question: Should peer review stay a strictly human sanctuary, adopt structured AI co-review loops, or hand first-pass evaluation to models?

pole_a.label: Human-only sanctuary
pole_a.summary: Uploading unpublished manuscripts risks leaking confidential work, invites generic rubber-stamped critiques, exposes venues to hidden prompt injection, and breaks human accountability for gatekeeping.

pole_b.label: Structured AI co-review & triage
pole_b.summary: Automated completeness checks, statistical/citation audits, and LLM review-feedback prompts (piloted at ICLR 2025) catch surface defects early and push human reviewers toward more concrete critiques.

fault_lines.hinge: Whether AI tools relieve reviewer burnout or accelerate mutual disengagement where AI writes, AI reviews, and nobody reads deeply.

fault_lines.question: Do mandatory AI-use declarations protect scholarly transparency, or do they punish conscientious authors while leaving bad actors untouched?

pole_a.label: Granular disclosure & audit
pole_a.summary: Editors and readers need explicit accounting of where generative tools shaped text, code, figures, or literature synthesis; undisclosed generation erodes trust in authorship.

pole_b.label: Drop prose policing
pole_b.summary: Unverifiable AI badges risk stigmatizing honest authors (especially non-native English writers), incentivize hiding routine use once LLMs sit inside every word processor, and distract from checking whether data and citations hold up.

fault_lines.hinge: Whether self-reported tool declarations carry real epistemic signal once generative assistance is embedded across everyday research software.

fault_lines.short: The slop commons vs. the equity dividend
fault_lines.question: Does near-zero marginal cost drown volunteer editors and reviewers, or does generative drafting level the global linguistic playing field?

pole_a.label: Tragedy of the review commons
pole_a.summary: Collapsing the time cost of plausible manuscripts fuels submission surges and industrial paper mills, exhausting unpaid reviewers and possibly pushing editors back toward institutional prestige heuristics.

pole_b.label: Dismantling the Anglophone tax
pole_b.summary: Multilingual scientists may spend far less energy fighting English idiom and surface bias against non-native phrasing, letting under-resourced labs compete on scientific substance.

fault_lines.hinge: Whether rising submission volume comes mainly from opportunistic volume maximization and paper mills or from previously excluded legitimate researchers.

fault_lines.question: Is LLM-assisted polishing flattening scientific voice, vocabulary, and conceptual diversity, or is it welcome clarity?

pole_a.label: Rhetorical & epistemic flattening
pole_a.summary: Measurable surges in model-favored vocabulary and uniform framing risk erasing disciplinary nuance and disguising weak study design behind confident fluency.

pole_b.label: Cleaner, faster communication
pole_b.summary: Clearer structure and standardized phrasing help readers and machines extract methods and findings quickly.

fault_lines.hinge: Whether convergence stays at surface word choice or quietly narrows which papers get cited and which interpretations look authoritative.

fault_lines.question: Do unvetted AI flags create reputational spam, or should autonomous AI pipelines scan millions of published papers to flag errors and fraud?

pole_a.label: Human-verified flags only
pole_a.summary: Broadcasting raw LLM error accusations across thousands of papers (as debated in 2025 viral error-hunting initiatives) can misread domain notation, harm innocent authors, and flood editors with false alarms.

pole_b.label: Archive-scale automated hygiene
pole_b.summary: Human sleuths can inspect only a sliver of the literature; automated checkers for hallucinated references, impossible statistics, image duplication, and tortured/synthetic text clean the record at scale.

fault_lines.hinge: How the community balances false negatives (undetected errors sitting in PubMed/arXiv) against false positives (publicly accusing authors over model misreadings).

fault_lines.question: Does scholarly communication cope by hardening traditional journal gates with human friction, or by unbundling the static journal article altogether?

pole_a.label: High-friction human gates
pole_a.summary: Submission caps, verified author identity, mandatory raw-data deposition, and preregistration aim to restore costly signals that synthetic mass production cannot fake cheaply.

pole_b.label: Preprints + continuous verification
pole_b.summary: Separate rapid open dissemination from layered evaluation (Publish-Review-Curate, funder-backed journal exits like Arcadia/Astera, and explicit agent-native venues like Agents4Science).

fault_lines.hinge: Whether journals still provide irreplaceable curation worth fortifying, or whether the static pre-publication journal bottleneck is itself obsolete.

models.name: AI Review-Critic & Bounded "Reviewer 4" Loops
models.tagline: Keep human editors and referees accountable while deploying auditable AI for technical checks and review-quality feedback
examples: ICLR 2025 / Nature Machine Intelligence randomized trial (~20,000 human reviews offered optional LLM feedback)
EMBO / Review Commons + qed author-centric pre-submission self-check survey and pilot (2026)
Nature Biotechnology "Reviewer 4" proposal, JAMA Network's stated plan to explore "driver-assistance" hybrid strategies, & OpenAI Prism Paper Review workflow (2025–2026)
Clinical-trial methodological error screeners tested on inserted RCT flaws (Brian et al. 2026 preprint)
models.mechanism: Manuscripts stay under human editorial accountability while bounded AI tools run consistency, statistical, and reporting checks — either upstream for authors before submission or alongside human referees as a non-voting technical report and review-specificity coach.
models.solves: Targets mechanical, arithmetic, and reporting omissions that time-pressed human referees miss while nudging vague two-line reviews toward concrete critique.
models.breaks_when: Reviewers rubber-stamp the AI report, LLMs invent plausible flaw lists on strong papers, or unlogged desk tools penalize non-Anglophone manuscripts without human override tracking.

models.name: Forensic Integrity Hubs & Adversarial Sanitization
models.tagline: Screen synthetic submissions, phantom citations, and prompt injections at manuscript ingestion — with human verification
examples: STM Integrity Hub & publisher paper-mill / review-mill screening pipelines
Screening for hidden white-font or micro-font PDF text aimed at LLM reviewers (recommended; a flagging tool for CHI 2027 is described secondhand)
Automated reference-existence cross-checks against bibliographic databases (~$0.04/paper API cost in one venue-scale scan, before human adjudication)
Proposed due-process safeguards for misconduct screening, with human verification and author reply (Hosseini & Resnik 2024/2025)
models.mechanism: Treats manuscript ingestion like cybersecurity with due process: flags invisible PDF prompt layers, cross-checks cited DOIs and titles against bibliographic registries, screens figures for duplication or generative artifacts, and routes candidate flags to human editors before any adverse decision.
models.solves: Flags candidate phantom citations and crude prompt injections before volunteer referee hours are spent.
models.breaks_when: Selected AI-manipulated Western blots and xenograft figures fool PhD readers near chance (50.5%), semantic rewrites evade surface filters, and unverified desk flags risk false accusations without transparent author appeal routes.

models.name: Costly-Signal & Scarcity Restoration
models.tagline: Reintroduce human bandwidth limits where prose fluency no longer filters effort
examples: American Journal of Political Science (AJPS) rolling 12-month cap of 3 submissions per author or co-author, with one annual waiver request (enacted 4 Nov 2026)
arXiv limit of 2 submissions per calendar month per submitter from October 2026 (up to 3 active submissions, a limit in place since 2024)
Individual proposal ahead of ICML 2027 for a human-reviewed conference track with a hard per-author cap beside an uncapped AI-reviewed track (Yona 2026)
models.mechanism: Because polished prose no longer signals scarce human labor, venues shift screening to resources that models cannot mint infinitely: rolling per-author submission budgets and capped human-reviewed tracks.
models.solves: Aims to cap zero-marginal-cost submission surges directly (effectiveness untested; arXiv calls its limit a stopgap) without relying on brittle AI-text classifiers or token watermarks.
models.breaks_when: Flat co-author caps squeeze large interdisciplinary labs and early-career collaborators.

models.name: Process Provenance ("Research Flight Recorders")
models.tagline: Move past binary AI-prose checkboxes toward workflow traces, raw-data archives, and formal verification
examples: End-to-end agent log traces, full hypothesis pools, and code-execution audits tested in PNAS (Luo, Kasirzadeh & Shah 2026) and proposed in Cell (Guo et al. 2026)
Funded archives of raw images, instrument outputs, and provenance metadata proposed in Nature (Shi, Nie & Kong 2026)

Proposed four-dimension AI disclosure in Pediatric Research (Coppes et al. 2026) & the proposed Resnik–Hosseini three-tier materiality framework vs. JACC's existing writing-only exemption (Krumholz 2026)
Registered Reports (Stage 1 pre-data acceptance) and Lean formal proof verification in mathematics and theoretical CS
models.mechanism: Audits how a study unfolded across hypotheses, raw instrument files, rejected runs, and formal proofs so editors and readers can inspect analytical choices that a polished manuscript PDF conceals.
models.solves: Targets post-hoc selection bias, undocumented data modifications, and low-information AI checkboxes (in one PNAS study of two AI-scientist systems, an LLM auditor's accuracy on a constructed benchmark rose from 53.7% to 81.5% when given logs and code).
models.breaks_when: High tooling friction outside computational fields; exploratory wet-lab science looks messy when surveilled commit-by-commit, and long-term raw-file repositories require sustained funder support.

models.name: Executable & Modular Research Packages
models.tagline: Treat static prose as a view layer over runnable code, primary data, and interactive paper-agents
examples: Paper2Agent (Nature 2026) converting 74 of 100 computational-biology papers into Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and interactive workflows
A partner's prototype for eLife mapping claims to evidence across ten of its neuroscience papers (2026)
Executable MyST / Curvenote / Jupyter-native articles
models.mechanism: Packages data, computational environments, code, and structured claim graphs alongside the narrative text so continuous integration and downstream readers can execute and inspect methods directly.
models.solves: Targets computational irreproducibility and separates executable verification from rhetorical polish, while human experts still guide open-ended biological validation. (For scale, on OpenAI's from-scratch PaperBench benchmark the best-scoring unaided agents reached 21.0–26.0% mean partial credit when re-implementing papers.)
models.breaks_when: Wet-lab, clinical, qualitative, and field sciences cannot reduce experimental validity to container re-execution, and agreement with reference outputs checks faithful execution without proving underlying scientific truth.

models.name: Publish-Review-Curate (PRC) + Open Audit Bots
models.tagline: Preprint openly, run specialized technical check-bots with human verification, and curate via editors
examples: eLife PRC model, Review Commons, PCI (Peer Community In), and Genomics x AI rapid community blog
QED Science scoring a year's worth of life-science preprints (57,455), by the developer's account (2026)
Specialized replication, formula, and reference screeners (Astra code-package auditor, GPT-6.1 Sol arXiv math scans, Problematic Paper Screener)
models.mechanism: Separates rapid open preprint dissemination from binary accept/reject gates; specialized screeners inspect code, proofs, reference tables, and citations while human editors verify flags and curate conceptual significance.
models.solves: Aims to reduce multi-journal rejection cascades where one flawed or synthetic manuscript burns several closed referee pools in sequence.
models.breaks_when: University hiring and grant panels still weight legacy journal mastheads, and broadcasting unverified bot flags risks reputational harm when models misread domain notation (F6).

models.name: Dedicated Agent-Native Venues & Sandboxes
models.tagline: Give autonomous AI research systems an explicit, labeled track for open stress-testing
examples: Stanford Agents4Science 2025 (>300 submissions, 48 accepted papers with AI first authors and AI reviewers on OpenReview)
Journal of AI Generated Papers (JAIGP, jaigp.org, launched by César A. Hidalgo in Feb 2026)

Sakana AI Scientist (Yamada et al. 2025; Lu et al. Nature 2026 — same human-filtered, protocol-withdrawn ICLR workshop test) & The Agentic Scientist (an Error Diffusion paper produced by human researchers using a development version, reported accepted at ALIFE 2026)
models.mechanism: Establishes dedicated conferences and journals explicitly labeled for AI-authored or AI-reviewed work so autonomous pipelines can be audited openly outside covert human-only queues.
models.solves: Provides a transparent sandbox for benchmarking agentic workflows, claim-level novelty filters (ClaimNov), and methodological failure modes without covert rule-breaking.
models.breaks_when: Critics warn dedicated AI venues normalize synthetic volume ("slop") or obscure heavy human steering behind nominal AI-authorship branding.

models.name: Institutional Journal Exit
models.tagline: Funders and institutes mandate open modular outputs and opt out of legacy journals
examples: Astera Institute policy ending funding and permission for traditional journal articles (in effect by June 2025)
Arcadia Science open modular publishing experiment (lessons analyzed 2023–2025)
Open hypothesis and modular release platforms bypassing journal cycles (2025–2026)
models.mechanism: Research funders remove the commercial journal incentive for their grantees — declining to pay APCs to publishers and funding immediate open datasets, code, and modular reports instead.
models.solves: Bypasses journal APCs, multi-month review queues, and prestige-driven narrative packaging for funded grantees.
models.breaks_when: Early-career researchers returning to conventional university departments face hiring and grant friction without journal lines, and self-hosted reports can struggle to attract independent external peer scrutiny.

sources.title: Guest Post — What AI Can’t Learn About Peer Review… Because Nobody Can Explain It
sources.summary: Drawing on semi-structured conversations with researchers and Taylor & Francis journal editors, Corless argues that expert peer review relies on tacit disciplinary judgment that resists rigid checklists, warning that AI-generated summaries can anchor what human referees notice even when humans hold the final judgement. The excerpt quotes interviewee Anja Baethge.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: As reviewers, we have so many quality criteria to assess a manuscript. But being an expert reviewer and defining ‘state of the art’ is not simply a matter of checking whether a paper meets each of these criteria. It’s deciding which criteria matter most and knowing how to weigh them.

sources.title: New AJPS Submission Cap Policy
sources.authors: American Journal of Political Science Editorial Team
sources.summary: Official 4 November 2026 policy announcement limiting individuals to authoring or co-authoring at most three AJPS submissions in any rolling 12-month period across articles, correspondence, and research notes, with one annual waiver request permitted for a fourth submission. Citing AI-accelerated output and a 19% mid-year submission rise from 2025 to 2026, the editors frame the cap as an initial step to protect finite editorial and reviewer capacity.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Individuals are allowed to author or co-author no more than three submissions to AJPS in any twelve month time period. Note that this is a rolling twelve month time period, and not a calendar year.

sources.title: The peer review paradox: How artificial intelligence is increasing the burden of scientific peer review
sources.summary: Argues that AI-driven submission growth increases the burden on peer reviewers while fewer journals permit AI in peer review than in manuscript preparation (citing copyright, quality and bias concerns), notes that publishers earn more as publication numbers rise, and proposes allowing AI across the editorial process, with authors who use AI consenting to its use in peer review.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: And despite journals allowing the use of AI in manuscript development with appropriate disclosures, substantially fewer journals allow AI use in peer review, largely citing copyright, quality, and potential bias concerns. This makes sense from a business perspective. Scientific publishing companies increase revenue with increased numbers of publications and associated article processing fees and journal subscriptions.

sources.title: “From now on I won't do any peer review without AI. For clinical trials, I'd even call human-only review dangerous”
sources.summary: Ruslan Rust argues, from his team's preprint, that human-only review of clinical trials is dangerous. His thread sets historical reviewer performance against the team's analysis of 58 recent trials, including eligible open-access phase 3 trials.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: TLDR: From now on I won't do any peer review without AI. For clinical trials, I'd even call human-only review dangerous

sources.title: AI Article Reviews Dominate Human Peer Reviews at Their Best: Evidence and Policy Choices
sources.summary: Working paper comparing AI reviews with 134 paid rapidPeer human reviews of 124 social-science manuscripts. Three former editors preferred AI in 26 of 30 judgments on the same ten review pairs, without being asked to read the manuscripts; most other evaluations used AI judges. The study measures review preferences and assessed claims, not subsequent manuscript improvements or publication decisions.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We show that AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors.

sources.title: Large language models detect methodological errors that human peer review misses in clinical trials
sources.authors: Dominikus Brian, Xavier Isidro Pereira Hernández, Hao Yin, Jeffrey Koury, Ruslan Rust
sources.summary: medRxiv v2 preprint testing 15 LLMs on inserted methodological errors: major-error scores of 53–96% on three historical trial reports (compared against a 27% mean among journal peer reviewers given no extra training in the original study) and 58–99% on recent trials, where the three highest-scoring frontier models were evaluated on only three of 58 recent trials (the posted medRxiv supplement archive reflects the initial 3-trial v1 release). Scoring used two LLM judges without contemporary human comparators, and models flagged 14–29% of tested error categories in unmodified control reports. Four of the five authors are affiliated with ResearchHub Foundation, which is implementing AI-assisted review.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: On the original reports, the models' major-error detection scores ranged from 53% to 96%. On the 2026 trials, scores ranged from 58% to 99%, and from 66% to 89% for the open-weight models. Notably, LLMs still flagged 14% to 29% of the error types in control reports without inserted errors

sources.title: AI-hallucinated citations should be treated as research misconduct
sources.summary: Nature correspondence, written after arXiv began banning papers with AI-hallucinated references, arguing that authors are accountable for every reference they cite and that hallucinated citations should be treated as research misconduct. The authors point to an Estonian administrative court that fined a party over a legal filing containing fabricated AI-generated academic references.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Authors — not AI tools — are accountable for every reference they cite. Hallucinated citations corrupt the scholarly record and should be treated as research misconduct, with consequences comparable to those of other serious breaches of research integrity.

sources.title: Do AI Scientists Know What's New?
sources.authors: Miri Liu, Xiayu Zhao, Encheng Xie, ChengXiang Zhai
sources.summary: Audits novelty filters on a controlled benchmark of 1,060 research proposals constructed around temporal cutoffs, finding that checks which reject most non-novel work also tend to raise false alarms on ideas that were later published (with exceptions), and introduces claim-level ClaimNov. Novelty labels are model-assisted, with a limited human audit.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Auditing existing novelty checks with this framework, we find that checks with high rejection rates on non-novel work also tend to have high false alarms on ideas that are later realized by human researchers.

sources.title: Evaluation of possibly fabricated references in 500,000 science, engineering, and computing papers
sources.authors: Maxim Topaz, Pallavi Gupta, Zhihong Zhang, Laura-Maria Peltonen
sources.summary: Auditing a stratified random sample of 500,000 peer-reviewed papers (January 2023–March 2026) across chemistry, physics, materials science, engineering, and computer science identified 1,135 fabricated references across 619 papers (85.8% precision on masked expert review), with affected-paper prevalence rising about 3.7-fold from 6.3 per 10,000 in 2023 to 23.0 per 10,000 in Q1 2026 (~8,500 papers extrapolated across 7M OpenAlex works). Fabricated is an operational verifiability label, not evidence of intent or AI causation; 18% of references lacked resolvable DOIs and were excluded, recall was not estimated, and the projection does not incorporate classification error.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Our automated pipeline classified 1,135 references across 619 papers as fabricated, with 85.8% precision on masked expert review; fabricated is an operational label for a claimed title that could not be located in any of seven bibliographic and open-web sources. Affected-paper prevalence rose from 1 in 1,600 (6.3 per 10,000) in 2023 to 1 in 435 (23.0 per 10,000) in the first quarter of 2026, and full-period rates differed roughly sixfold across fields, from 25.6 per 10,000 papers in physics to 4.3 in chemistry.

sources.title: Attitudes and perceptions toward the use of artificial intelligence chatbots for peer review in medical journals: a large-scale, international cross-sectional survey
sources.authors: Jeremy Y. Ng, Daivat Bhavsar, Neha Dhanvanthry, Lex Bouter, Teresa Chan, Holger Cramer, Annette Flanagin, Alfonso Iorio, Cynthia Lokker, Hervé Maisonneuve, Ana Marušić, David Moher
sources.summary: International survey of medical-journal peer reviewers (1,077 answered the main questions; 1.9% response rate). Most were familiar with AI chatbots (86.2%) and used them for general purposes (87.7%), yet 70.3% had not used them for peer review and 69.5% said their institutions offered no training on it. Concerns about algorithmic bias (80.3%) and trust (73.3%) were widespread.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: While familiarity with AICs is high among medical journal peer reviewers, their reported use in peer review remains limited. There is clear interest in training and guidance, however, concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and research integrity persist and should be addressed before broader implementation.

sources.title: Giving AI a seat at the peer review table
sources.summary: Proposes adding AI to manuscript and grant peer review as a bounded, non-voting, secure and auditable ‘Reviewer 4’ that writes a report (on conceptual advance and novelty, methods, data and statistics) without issuing a recommendation, so that voting authority stays with the human referees.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: There is an opportunity here to refocus and strengthen the process of peer review, with AI as a bounded, non-voting, secure, auditable tool — not replacing scientists, but serving as an additional ‘Reviewer 4’.

sources.title: What genomics and big data science can teach us about authorship in the era of generative AI
sources.summary: Responding to Earp and colleagues' proposal to disaggregate authorship, this bioethics essay argues for keeping the ICMJE's four authorship criteria, which leave generative AI outside accountable authorship. Drawing on large genomics and data-science programmes, where many contributors cannot meet all four criteria, it argues that contributor statements should be visible, indexed and counted in hiring and promotion.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Large biomedical research programmes, especially genomics and data science, typically distribute these functions across multidisciplinary teams, making it difficult for many researchers to satisfy all four ICMJE criteria. Generative AI makes it even more challenging now, as it separates authorial functions across humans and machines.

sources.title: Opus 4.8 outperforming human expert peer reviewers across 124 Harvard social-science papers
sources.summary: Ethan Mollick highlights a Harvard working paper comparing reviews of 124 social-science manuscripts and urges academia to adapt rapidly to AI.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: By every measure, Opus 4.8 beats human experts as peer reviewers in a study of 124 Harvard social science papers covering a range from statistical analyses to formal models to qualitative work. As academics, we need to figure out how to adapt the practice of science to AI, fast.

sources.title: ICLR reviewer pushback: allow AI in research, ban AI in writing papers
sources.summary: Darshil Doshi, after reviewing for ICLR, argues that the only remaining way to save peer review is to ban AI from writing papers while allowing it in research.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: After hours of playing guess-what-is-AI-slop (aka reviewing for @iclr_conf ), I am convinced that the only Hail Mary left to save peer review is to fully ban AI usage in *writing* papers. Use AI for research, but communication has to be fully human.

sources.title: Could an unpublished idea typed into a chatbot or coding agent end up with the company or a rival?
sources.summary: News teaser asking whether an unpublished idea typed into a chatbot or coding agent could end up being used by the company that built the model or by a rival, noting that no setting makes a chatbot fully private and that experts suggest steps to make leaks less likely.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: When you type an unpublished idea into a chatbot or coding agent, could it end up being used by the company that built the model—or a rival who asks the right question a year later?

sources.title: How we’re approaching AI at bioRxiv and medRxiv
sources.summary: openRxiv sets out its approach to AI at bioRxiv and medRxiv: authors must be verifiable, affiliated humans who stand behind their work; submissions showing uncritical AI output, such as many fabricated references or wholly AI-written conclusions, may be declined; authors can be rate-limited and machine access restricted; and automated screening tools never decide alone. It also recognizes AI as a useful drafting aid, especially for non-native English speakers.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: When screening identifies evidence that authors have not critically reviewed AI-generated material, such as large numbers of fabricated references or entirely AI-generated discussion/conclusions, a submission may receive further review and we reserve the right to decline the work.

sources.title: GPT-6.1 Sol auditing ~800 arXiv math papers: “cleaning up decades of human slop”
sources.summary: Commentary on an automated audit of nearly 800 mathematics preprints that reports major errors in 6% of them and an estimated 90% precision for its major findings. The original post it quotes compares 6% main-theorem flags before August 2026 with 1.5% in two later months.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: gpt-6.1 sol examined nearly 800 mathematics papers, finding major errors in 6% and minor mistakes in another 30%. researchers estimate that 90% of its major findings are correct — i'm glad AI is now cleaning up decades of human slop

sources.title: ArXiv versus AI slop: will capping preprint submissions work?
sources.summary: Nature news report on arXiv's cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher, in force since 1 October 2026 after a surge that arXiv's scientific director attributes mainly to AI slop (40,000 preprints in September, up from about 30,000 a month earlier in the year). Researchers quoted call the cap reasonable, point out that co-authors can take turns to submit, or warn that rejected papers will simply go elsewhere; SocArXiv now allows one article per author per week.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In a bid to tackle the deluge of manuscripts it now receives, the preprint server arXiv has announced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher, which began on 1 October.

sources.title: Preserve research data for tomorrow's AI-enabled integrity checks
sources.authors: Qingde Shi, Jinlei Nie, Zhaowei Kong
sources.summary: Nature correspondence responding to reports of AI tools finding long-standing errors in published papers. Drawing on how anti-doping agencies store samples, the authors propose funded long-term archives of original images, instrument outputs, metadata and provenance records, so that future AI-assisted integrity checks can inspect the primary evidence.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Anti-doping offers a useful precedent: blood and urine samples can be stored for up to ten years and retested if detection methods improve. The same idea could be applied to research: preserving data now allows findings to be reassessed using better methods later.

sources.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
sources.authors: Robert Tjarko Lange, Luca Grillotti, Yutaro Yamada, Rujikorn Charakorn, David Ha
sources.summary: Sakana AI preprint introducing ‘The Agentic Scientist’ (code repository: AI Scientist v3), orchestrating multi-agent coding, baseline and ablation construction, rubric self-verification, and report drafting across an autonomy spectrum; in its human–AI co-scientist setting, the authors used a development version to submit a single research paper (on Error Diffusion) that they report was accepted at ALIFE 2026.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026.

sources.title: Emerging math/CS swarm research: “Lean replaces peer review… Agent legibility > human legibility”
sources.summary: Observes, about a community auto-research effort on integer multiplication, that “it feels like a new kind of academia is emerging”, listing features such as Lean replacing peer review and agent legibility outranking human legibility. This is one observer’s description of a trend, not advocacy or evidence that it works.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Reading this, it feels like a new kind of academia is emerging. - Anyone with extra LLM usage can contribute - Lean replaces peer review - Orchestrated on anonymous group chats - Much faster but in more incremental steps - Agent legibility > human legibility

sources.title: AI in Medical Writing: Why JACC Does Not Require Disclosure
sources.summary: October 2026 editorial explaining JACC's existing writing-assistance policy (set out in a 2025 Editor’s Page), which departs from the January 2026 ICMJE update reaffirming that journals should require disclosure: AI used solely to improve writing requires no disclosure when human authors stand behind every word, whereas AI used in conducting the research must be reported in Methods for reproducibility, and reviewer confidentiality duties stay strict.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: This Editor’s Page is not about a change in JACC policy. Rather, it is a fuller account of why we draw the line where we do and what we require instead. This policy does not apply to AI used in the conduct of the research, which should be reported as part of the scientific methods.

sources.title: The more you automate, the less you see: Hidden pitfalls of autonomous AI scientists
sources.authors: Ziming Luo, Atoosa Kasirzadeh, Nihar B. Shah
sources.summary: Controlled symbolic-reasoning experiments on Agent Laboratory and AI Scientist v2 found benchmark-selection bias, undocumented data changes and post-hoc selection based on test performance. They did not find clear test-set peeking or deliberate metric gaming. On a balanced audit dataset mixing natural and deliberately introduced failures, a rule-guided LLM auditor improved from 53.7% accuracy with manuscripts alone to 81.5% with logs and code. This supports process transparency, with generalization beyond these systems and tasks still untested.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Crucially, we find that these flaws are largely invisible at the level of the final manuscript, suggesting that current manuscript-centric peer review paradigms are fundamentally insufficient for ensuring the integrity of automated research.

sources.title: Against mandatory prompt disclosure in AI-assisted scholarship
sources.authors: Brian D. Earp, Udo Schüklenk, Julian Savulescu, Sebastian Porsdam Mann
sources.summary: Argues against mandatory inclusion of all prompts and outputs for ordinary writing assistance, citing enforceability, burden, equity and surveillance concerns. Explicitly supports normalized AI-use declarations, targeted methods-level documentation when validity or reproducibility requires it, voluntary records, and human authorship attestation.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We argue, however, against Mandatory Full Inclusion (MFI) of prompts and outputs for ordinary writing assistance. Such a policy would, we suggest, be difficult to enforce, easy for dishonest users to evade, burdensome for careful users to follow, and poorly suited to the capacities of editors and peer reviewers.

sources.title: Biomedical Research Images Manipulated by Generative AI to Alter Scientific Outcomes: Diagnostic Study of Human and Automated Detection
sources.authors: Shuhang Luo, Runhua Tang, Ziyin Chen, Jianye Wang, Ming Liu, Jianfeng Wang, Li Ma
sources.summary: Controlled diagnostic study of 52 authentic and 52 matched, selected AI-manipulated Western blot and xenograft tumor images (with failed generations excluded and each of 24 PhD-level biomedical reviewers judging a 50-image sample): human accuracy averaged 50.5% (SD 6.9%) and the top tested commercial detector reached AUC 0.790 across the two evaluated image modalities.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In a diagnostic study of 104 western blot and subcutaneous xenograft tumor images, a high-fidelity generative model produced forgeries that could alter the conclusions of a study; 24 PhD-level expert reviewers could not reliably distinguish the forgeries from authentic figures (mean accuracy 50.5%, SD 6.9%), while the best-performing commercial AI detector achieved only moderate discrimination (area under the curve 0.790, 95% CI 0.695-0.885), revealing critical vulnerabilities in current research-integrity safeguards.

sources.title: Fair Moderation, Equitable Access, and AI: arXiv’s Updated Rate Limit Policy
sources.summary: Announces a rate limit of two submissions per calendar month per submitter, alongside the existing limit (in place since 2024) of three active submissions at a time, after monthly arXiv submissions doubled in two years from 20,569 (September 2024) to 40,363 (September 2026).
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In September of 2016, arXiv received 9,869 submissions. In September of 2024, arXiv received 20,569 submissions. This September, arXiv received 40,363 submissions, which in turn generated almost 9,000 support tickets for arXiv staff and moderators. In only the past two years, submissions have doubled.

sources.title: “Claude-shaped science”: an impedance mismatch between LLM strengths and human-collaborator-style workflows
sources.authors: Anthropic (@AnthropicAI), on a guest post by Matthew Schwartz
sources.summary: Anthropic promotes a guest essay by physicist Matthew Schwartz, a visiting researcher at Anthropic, on matching scientific work to what language models do well, such as exact calculations and expert-steered exploration. One example is an AI data editor that ported the replication packages of 4,452 papers in five leading economics journals to open-source code and checked them against the published tables (NBER working paper w35782).
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In physics, an “impedance mismatch” occurs when two systems each work well but are poorly matched. In this Science Blog guest post, Harvard physicist Matthew Schwartz argues that something similar is happening with AI and science.

sources.title: Peer Review Should Start With AI
sources.summary: Grünebaum proposes mandatory, documented AI review inside a confidential journal environment ahead of human refereeing, keeping final editorial decisions in human hands while citing King and Worthington's 26-of-30 editor preference result across ten social-science pairs and noting its bounded non-clinical scope.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Every manuscript must get an AI review before it reaches a human reviewer, and that review must be part of the official record.

sources.title: The Gate Before Peer Review
sources.summary: Agarwal argues for measurable human oversight of automated desk screening: override rates, appeals, disclosure of who is responsible for a decision, and a chance to fix compliance problems. He warns that automated screening can create language-related inequity and predicts that editors will rarely override it.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: A person can sit inside a process and still not be exercising much judgement.

sources.title: Why LLM referees never say “accept as is”: the laundry-list-of-flaws bias
sources.summary: Andrew Rosen argues that an LLM asked to review a manuscript or proposal will always produce a ‘laundry list’ of flaws, even for excellent work, and that these flaws can look sensible while being low-quality.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: when asked to review a manuscript or proposal, an LLM will never say "this looks great, accept as is." It will *always* come up with a laundry list of "flaws", even for excellent work. These flaws can be superficially sensible but actually low-quality.

sources.title: Proposal for two conference tracks, one AI-reviewed and uncapped, one human-reviewed and capped, citing 60,000 ICLR submissions
sources.authors: Gal Yona (@_galyo), quoting Andrew Gordon Wilson (@andrewgwils)
sources.summary: Gal Yona, answering an ICML 2027 program chair's call for ideas and citing 60,000 ICLR submissions, proposes two parallel conference tracks: an uncapped track reviewed and judged by AI, and a human-reviewed track with a hard cap on submissions per author.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: desperate times call for desperate measures, and as the 60k ICLR submissions show, the ML community has been too slow to rise to the challenge.

sources.title: Nathan Lambert on LLM-supervised peer review: “If we don’t solve it the academic institutions are toast”
sources.summary: Nathan Lambert calls LLM-supervised peer review one of the most important research problems for computer-science academics, warns that academic institutions are ‘toast’ if it is not solved, and judges it easier than building new institutions.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Seems like one of the most important research problems for CS academics is llm-supervised peer review. If we don’t solve it the academic institutions are toast. It seems easier than building new institutions.

sources.title: Toward autonomous science with agentic artificial intelligence
sources.authors: Lucie Y. Guo, Darren S.J. Ting, Xinyi Su, Alex Aliper, Alex Zhavoronkov, Daniel S.W. Ting
sources.summary: Cell Perspective tracing agentic AI in biomedicine from image classifiers to multi-agent ‘co-scientists’ such as Co-Scientist, Robin and Biomni, which generate hypotheses, design experiments and refine their reasoning from experimental results. The authors argue that AI's potential is inseparable from problems of hallucination, bias, irreproducibility and dual use. Two of the authors are executives of Insilico Medicine.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: This perspective traces the emergence of agentic scientific reasoning, discusses scaling laws and autonomous laboratories, and argues that AI’s transformative potential is inseparable from challenges in hallucination, bias, irreproducibility, and dual use.

sources.title: Reimagining research papers as interactive and reliable AI agents
sources.authors: Jiacheng Miao, Joe R. Davis, Yaohui Zhang, Jonathan K. Pritchard, James Zou
sources.summary: Paper2Agent turns a published paper, its code and its data into an AI agent built on Model Context Protocol tools. It converted 74 of 100 computational-biology papers. On 300 tutorial-derived questions, checked against the outputs of the original code, the agents reached 91.2% accuracy, against 80.3% for Claude Code with direct repository access on the same model (Sonnet 4) and 86.3% on Sonnet 4.6. Reproducing a paper's outputs tests faithful execution of its code, and open-ended discovery with the agents stayed human-steered.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Paper2Agent addresses this challenge by converting a paper into an AI agent that functions as a virtual corresponding author, exposing its manuscript, supplementary materials, datasets, code and workflows as active, agent-native knowledge rather than static text. It analyses the paper and codebase using multiple agents to construct a model context protocol (MCP) server, then generates and runs tests to refine and increase robustness of the MCP.

sources.title: Use and Effects of LLMs in Peer Review: A Randomized Experiment and Survey at ICML 2026
sources.authors: Sunnie S. Y. Kim, Wesley Hanwen Deng, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan, Buxin Su, Weijie Su, Alekh Agarwal, Sharon Li, Martin Jaggi, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nihar B. Shah, Miroslav Dudík
sources.summary: ICML 2026 randomly switched 10% of the 16,877 main-track papers whose authors allowed LLM-assisted review (1,686 papers) to a no-LLM policy, and randomly assigned a subset of reviewers willing to work under either policy. The policy made almost no difference to acceptance (27.0% vs 26.5%), scores or reviewer confidence; reviews under the permissive policy were 5.5–7% longer. In an anonymous survey (1,486 responses), 22.5% of reviewers under the ban said they had used an LLM anyway, and 36.5% under the permissive policy reported at least one disallowed use.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Policy assignment had near-zero effects on final paper decisions, paper scores, and reviewer confidence, although reviews under the permissive policy were 5.5-7% longer.

sources.title: Guest Post — Peer Review Triage: Deciding What’s Worth Saving
sources.summary: Cites a roughly 68% rise in submissions between 2018 and 2025 (from a Silverchair report), about 2.5 desk rejections per acceptance in 2025 and a 22.3% reviewer acceptance rate in 2024. Swain names AI-assisted writing, on top of publication pressure, as one big driver of the overload, and advocates integrity tools alongside stronger reviewer relationships.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: One big driver is the ubiquity of AI-assisted writing tools, sitting on top of a pressure-filled culture where PhD students and early career researchers are asked to double their outputs to advance their careers. The incentive to publish more collides with a technology that makes writing and publishing easier to do.

sources.title: AI watermarks do not measure intellectual contribution: Implications for academic publishing
sources.summary: Earp shares a paper titled “AI watermarks do not measure intellectual contribution: Implications for academic publishing”, written after Anthropic announced that its models will introduce watermarks.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: AI watermarks do not measure intellectual contribution: Implications for academic publishing

sources.title: Crémieux: an Astra run on replication packages “found a huge number of coding errors”, some said to overturn central results
sources.summary: Crémieux reports that running Astra on a batch of replication packages turned up many coding errors, most of them inconsequential and some, he says, overturning central results of papers in high-ranking journals.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: I sicced Astra on a bunch of replication packages, and it found a huge number of coding errors. Most of these were inconsequential, but some of them overturn central results for papers in high-ranking journals.

sources.title: Ready for the robot reviewers?
sources.summary: Science news feature (DOI 10.1126/science.aem0443; web edition 10.1126/science.z6vx92p) examining reviewer uptake of AI amid surging submissions and referee fatigue — including NEJM AI’s fast track, in which an editor reviews selected manuscripts in full without AI and editors then weigh the human and AI reviews — alongside AI's verbosity, nitpicking, and weakness on conceptual novelty.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: As AI’s capabilities grow, researchers and publishers are exploring how it can support peer review—and where it still falls short

sources.title: Who is responsible when AI helps to write science?
sources.summary: Nature Comment on who bears responsibility when generative AI helps to write science: Braun argues that generative AI cannot take responsibility for what it produces and proposes a CRediT-style statement of AI use in which verification and accountability stay with the human author. An end-note states that ChatGPT 5.4 was used as a dialogical writing and analytical aid and Claude 4.2 to review the article.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: GenAI (OpenAI ChatGPT 5.4) was used as a dialogical writing and analytical aid during the development of the piece, including for idea generation, structural iteration, prose generation, summarization, condensation and stylistic revision. It also assisted in synthesizing relationships between the cited papers and the author’s uploaded manuscripts. GenAI (Anthropic Claude 4.2) was used to review the article.

sources.title: Journal editor testimony: disclosed AI “language refinement” obscuring promising studies beneath over-complex text
sources.summary: Williamson reports editorial experience of promising studies obscured by excessive AI-assisted language revision and calls for better writing support, especially for early-career and non-Anglophone authors.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: What's most upsetting me as a journal editor is that many papers we receive where AI use is disclosed for editing and language refinement actually appear to have been ruined rather than improved by AI. We receive what seem like promising underpinning studies, but which are totally obscured by over-complex text.

sources.title: Has the Scientific Paper Become Too Big for Human Peer Review?
sources.summary: Di Carlo proposes separating concise scientific narratives from structured evidence bases, with AI doing the exhaustive checking and experts the scientific judgement. He describes two recent manuscripts whose reviews he suspects were written with AI, argues that today's papers have outgrown what human reviewers can check, and acknowledges risks to confidentiality, bias and excessive criticism.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: AI performs the exhaustive review. The expert performs the scientific judgment.

sources.title: MIT guidance against relying on AI text detectors over adversarial arms-race dynamics
sources.summary: Rohan Paul discusses a reported MIT recommendation against relying on AI detectors in education, citing evasion, false-positive harm and distrust. This social post is secondary commentary; the scope of the institutional recommendation requires the underlying report.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: The AI detector industry should be very uncomfortable reading this MIT report. The strongest institutional rejections yet, direct from MIT. "we recommend against relying on AI detectors."

sources.title: Publisher split: a philosophy-journal editor who does not want AI-written manuscripts vs. Elsevier's accountability-centered policy
sources.summary: Contrasts a philosophy-journal editor who said he did not want AI-written manuscripts with Elsevier's August 2026 policy update ('Authors are welcome to use AI, while remaining accountable'), under which authors verify facts and sources, review and edit AI output, and disclose AI use when required.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Elsevier’s approach is essentially to require authors to remain responsible for what they write: verify the facts and sources, review and edit AI-generated output, make sure the paper reflects their own analysis and ideas, and disclose the use of AI when required.

sources.title: The future of peer review requires AI support, not AI bans
sources.summary: Nature correspondence arguing that blanket journal bans on reviewer AI use protect confidentiality and accountability imperfectly and are hard to monitor, and calling on journals to offer safeguards and reviewer-friendly AI services, on publishers to set standards and build secure, purpose-built AI infrastructure, and on the AI industry to help.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Confidential manuscripts should not be exposed to public AI systems, and reviewers must remain accountable for their assessment. Yet blanket bans address concerns imperfectly and are hard to monitor.

sources.title: The shrinking landscape of linguistic diversity in the age of large language models
sources.authors: Zhivar Sourati, Farzan Karimi-Malekabadi, Meltem Ozcan, Colin McDaniel, Alireza Ziabari, Jackson Trager, Ala N. Tak, Meng Chen, Fred Morstatter, Morteza Dehghani
sources.summary: Combines observational corpus analysis with controlled rewriting experiments. In 1,000 pre-ChatGPT arXiv abstracts and 1,000 Reddit stories, rewriting usually reduced aggregate writing-complexity variance, with exceptions by model and prompt. Trait classifiers generally lost predictive accuracy while remaining above baseline; these are changes in textual signals, not demonstrated changes in people or cognition. In our reading, some of the published supplementary statistics are internally inconsistent.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Across three studies spanning seven datasets in different domains and over 880,000 texts, we show that the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) as writing assistants is linked to declines in linguistic diversity, interfering with the societal and psychological insights language provides. While core content is retained when LLMs polish and rewrite texts, LLMs also homogenize writing styles, reducing writing-complexity variance by a statistically significant 21–50% across datasets and models (P ≤ 0.05), and amplify patterns associated with dominant characteristics while suppressing others, emphasizing conformity over individuality.

sources.title: Peer review without the expert: artificial intelligence-assisted reviewing and the cost to science
sources.summary: Opinion article in Heart examining referee reports the authors consider most likely LLM-generated (verified from the publisher's opening preview paragraph; subsequent paragraphs remain behind subscription), describing uniformly polished reports whose objections look plausible at first glance yet stay conceptually shallow, penalize lesser-known methods, and repeat identical misreadings across supposedly independent reviews.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: The text is uniformly polished. The objections are plausible on first reading and conceptually shallow on inspection. The development and use of lesser-known methods is flagged as a methodological weakness rather than recognised as the contribution.

sources.title: Acceleration of the arms race between fraudsters and honest researchers
sources.summary: Bishop recounts a manuscript purporting to analyse her own data that required unavailable record linkage and supplied non-functional code. She regards it as fabricated, suspects AI involvement, argues for checks of data, code and citations, and doubts that automated screening will be enough.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: I have strong doubts as to whether the world of academic publishing is ready for this, and I'm not confident that any kind of AI-screening will cope with the more sophisticated kinds of AI-fraud. I cling to the faint hope that human experts still might be able to trap some of it, but I'm feeling more and more like a member of the Light Brigade, galloping into the Valley of Death-of-Research-Credibility.

sources.title: eLife Latest: Exploring AI’s potential for improving research engagement
sources.summary: eLife describes three AI projects built on its open peer reviews: OpenEval, which extracted results across the whole eLife corpus; Zachary Mainen's claim-tree prototype, which turned 10 neuroscience papers into 173 linked claims; and a small opt-in pilot with QED Science, in which reviewers judged about 80% of their comments correctly assigned to the AI-extracted claims. eLife argues for machine-readable claims alongside narrative papers and notes that Preprints.ai is not one of its partnerships.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: While human reviews and AI-generated claim structures differ significantly, the goal was to test whether this new communication format could help bring them together.

sources.title: Scientific production in the era of large language models: Outcome-triggered treatment timing and spurious event-study dynamics
sources.authors: Thomas Renault, Antonin Bergeaud, Clément Bosquet
sources.summary: Reanalyzing Kusumegi et al. (2025) with reconstructed arXiv data, simulations and four placebo tests (random treatment assignment, neutral-keyword triggers, inverted treatment, and pre-ChatGPT placebo periods) shows that dating LLM adoption by the first paper detected as LLM-assisted ties treatment to high-output months and generates spurious post-adoption productivity gains. First posted as an arXiv comment (May 2026); published in PNAS in August 2026.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Using reconstructed arXiv data, we show that random treatment assignments, neutral-keyword triggers, inverted treatment, and pre-ChatGPT placebo periods all generate similar dynamics. Simulations with no treatment effect also reproduce the same posttreatment patterns reported in K. Kusumegi et al., Science 390, 1240–1243 (2025).

sources.title: Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing
sources.authors: Lena Holzwarth, Rita González-Márquez, Dmitry Kobak
sources.summary: Extending unbiased excess word-frequency estimation from abstracts to full-text open-access biomedical articles in PubMed Central estimates that by December 2025, 89% of papers (77% across all of 2025) display excess LLM-associated vocabulary. Paragraph-level prevalence is twice as high in Discussion sections (68%) as in Methods sections (32%), and overall Methods-section prevalence exceeds 50%.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We apply our method to the full texts of open-access biomedical papers from Pubmed Central, and show that by the end of 2025, 89% of papers show excess of LLM-associated vocabulary. We also find that LLMs are twice as likely to be used when writing a paragraph in the Discussion section (68%) compared to a paragraph in the Methods section (32%), but even inside the Methods section, the overall prevalence of LLM usage is over 50%.

sources.title: Disputed AI-authorship claim: Pangram classification cited as rating a paper presented as “single-authored” by Claude as 82% human-written
sources.summary: Análise Real questions a claim that Claude was the sole author of a paper, citing a Pangram score that classed 82% of it as human-written, and asks Anthropic to clarify how two named colleagues edited the manuscript. In a reply, one of them describes steering Claude through rounds of feedback without editing the text directly. Detector scores like this one cannot settle authorship.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: According to @pangram, 82% of the paper presented as “single-authored” by Claude is classified as human-written.

sources.title: This AI tool claims to pick the top 1% of preprints. Should researchers trust it?
sources.summary: Nature Q&A with Niv Mastboim, co-founder and chief executive of QED Science, whose AI tool ranked more than 57,000 bioRxiv preprints by originality and validity and selected a ‘top 1%’; bioRxiv's operator is piloting it. Mastboim says the company offers free services to authors, not to journals, and that blinded experts preferred the QED-favoured paper in 75% of decisive disagreements with journal rank. The introduction notes concerns that the ranking creates another badge of prestige.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: A growing number of private firms are offering researchers artificial-intelligence tools for scrutinizing manuscripts before publication. One such system, developed by a start-up called QED Science in Tel Aviv, Israel, aims to judge whether life-sciences research is original and valid.

sources.title: AI agents are checking the scientific literature — and spotting decades-old errors
sources.summary: Nature news report on AI tools that check published papers and reference databases for errors, including wrong boiling points in a 75-year-old reference database exposed when an AI prediction model disagreed with it. Nature reports a survey of 733 ICML 2026 submitters in which 35% said Google's Paper Assistant Tool found errors in their work; researchers quoted warn of false positives and invented problems.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: For decades, chemists have relied on handbook values for a molecule’s boiling point to identify substances and plan processes such as distillation. But an artificial-intelligence model has revealed that some trusted numbers in one reference database have been wrong all along.

sources.title: ‘A waste of time for all of us’: caught in the crossfire of the peer-review wars
sources.summary: Nature investigates duplicate review reports and coercive citation requests, including the consequences of integrity notices for authors who rejected inappropriate requests. The feature reports documented examples, disputed allegations and publisher responses. AI is discussed as a possible facilitator of generic reviews, not demonstrated as their cause; open-review availability affects which publishers can be investigated.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: “There should be more publishing of peer reviews, precisely because it is one way to be aware of this phenomenon,” Bishop says. The growing use of artificial-intelligence tools probably contributes, too, as they make it easy to produce generic review content.

sources.title: AI Didn't Break Scientific Publishing. It Exposed What Was Already Broken.
sources.summary: Okoro analyses 65,039 retraction records from January 2006 to August 2026, grouped by retraction date and using a broad reason code for computer-generated content, and argues for verifiable data, code and provenance alongside responsible AI use.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Scientific integrity depends on everyone involved in the publication process, not only the authors.

sources.title: As AI writing proliferates academics should publish less
sources.summary: Argues that generative AI has cut the effort cost that once made publication counts a noisy but meaningful proxy for research effort. Proposes a systemic, field-calibrated cap (possibly averaged over several years) on the total number of papers any researcher can co-author across all venues so scarcity shifts back to human judgment.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Once much of the labour of producing a paper can be automated, as it increasingly can, a long publication list stops being evidence of anything except a willingness to keep submitting. The reward system, still built around counting, has not caught up.

sources.title: AI in scientific publishing: Slower, worse, and more expensive
sources.summary: Science editorial comparing AI in publishing to industrial Taylorism: against promises that AI makes work faster, better and cheaper, the rigorous human checking that AI-generated research papers require is creating bottlenecks that make scientific publishing slower and more expensive.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Indeed, scientific publishing is starting to experience some Taylorism with the insertion of AI. Rigorous human checking of AI-generated research papers is creating bottlenecks as publishers strive to maintain the integrity of the scientific record. The challenge is requiring even more human effort, making the whole endeavor slower and more expensive.

sources.title: Ethics journal retracts paper by high school student for AI, peer review manipulation
sources.summary: Reports a Journal of Medical Ethics retraction citing unverified AI-assisted references and evidence of peer-review manipulation. The author agreed to retraction. The report separately investigates affiliations on another paper by the same author; those affiliation concerns should not be conflated with the stated grounds for the ethics-paper retraction.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: “The journal investigated concerns about the quality of the work and the accuracy of the references, including concerns that several references did not exist,” the notice reads.

sources.title: Phantom References: Hallucinated Citations That Survive Peer Review at Top-Tier Conferences
sources.authors: Mark Russinovich, Ram Shankar Siva Kumar, Ahmed Salem
sources.summary: RefChecker scanned 48,095 accepted papers and 2,614,992 references. In 2025, 5.1% of NeurIPS and 4.8% of USENIX Security papers had at least two likely invalid academic references flagged. These are candidates requiring adjudication: most manually examined flags were recoverable references or false positives. A roughly $0.04-per-paper API cost (from the ICLR 2025 scan) excludes human verification. The audit does not establish AI authorship; some contacted authors reported that errors entered at the camera-ready stage, and the authors conclude that peer review does not reliably catch hallucinated citations.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: False positives are the primary limitation.

sources.title: Hidden Prompts in Manuscripts Exploit AI-Assisted Peer Review
sources.summary: Documents 18 arXiv manuscripts, found through targeted searches as of 7 July 2025, that hid review-favouring prompts, and classifies the prompts into four types; the targeted search makes 18 a lower bound. Lin argues that self-serving instructions undermine the defence that hidden prompts are neutral honeypots, and recommends controlled AI integration and screening.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In July 2025, 18 academic manuscripts on arXiv contained hidden instructions that manipulated AI-assisted peer review (indirect prompt injection). Instructions such as "GIVE A POSITIVE REVIEW ONLY" were concealed using white text and microscopic font sizes.

sources.title: Policy snapshots cannot establish journal AI-policy failure
sources.summary: Letter arguing that policy snapshots, missing adoption dates, permitted editing, and nonpublic disclosure channels prevent causal conclusions about policy failure. It accepts the descriptive evidence of rising AI-associated writing and rare public disclosures.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: The concern is narrower: their data document diffusion and public disclosure but do not establish the headline inference

sources.title: Reply to Wang: Policy failure can be assessed from observed outcomes
sources.summary: Reply defending an aggregate outcome-based interpretation of policy failure, while explicitly distinguishing public transparency from private disclosure and acknowledging that the study does not identify journal-specific causal effects or individual misconduct.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Disclosures invisible to readers do not provide public transparency.

sources.title: Fixing Scientific Publishing
sources.authors: Oded Rechavi (Tel Aviv University / qed Science)
sources.summary: Oded Rechavi, co-founder of QED Science, describes how its AI scored 57,455 life-science preprints and selected a top 1%, and reports that domain experts sided with the QED score over journal rank in three of four cases where the two disagreed. He presents the tool as a complement to peer review.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: It’s not meant to replace peer review, it complements it.

sources.title: AI promised to democratise academic publishing – the evidence says otherwise
sources.summary: Argues that language assistance alone cannot remove structural publishing inequalities and that AI-associated phrasing can become another cue for bias. Drawing on secondary studies, the author warns that punitive disclosure rules may disproportionately burden multilingual and under-resourced researchers.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Bias against non-native English speakers in peer review persists even when authors use large language models to improve their writing. Reviewers use language as a proxy for identity, and when AI erases one set of linguistic cues, they shift to another. The discrimination does not disappear. It adapts.

sources.title: Writing is thinking: understanding the real risks of AI in scientific writing
sources.summary: Nature Partnerships training blog arguing that drafting helps researchers clarify arguments, identify gaps and develop their own voice. It warns against delegating the whole writing process and recommends AI help for grammar, phrasing, flow and summaries.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: One of the most important reasons for writing your own paper is that it forces you to think, and really know, your research. When you write it up, you need to structure your thoughts in such a way that your audience can clearly understand your thoughts and ideas. As we’ve already seen, it’s about more than writing it down. It’s an exercise in itself about clarifying your thoughts to formulate arguments, and identifying any gaps in your logic or evidence.

sources.title: Genomics × AI community blog: sharing incremental and negative results fast without waiting on publishers
sources.summary: Alan Murphy promotes the Genomics × AI community blog, where the genomics and machine-learning community shares incremental results, negative results and tutorials quickly and discusses them “without waiting on a publisher”.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We built the Genomics × AI blog so the genomics + ML community can share work fast and actually discuss it — incremental results, negative results, tutorials — without waiting on a publisher.

sources.title: AI in peer review: the elephant in the editorial room
sources.authors: Giusy Rita Maria La Rosa, Mona Nasser
sources.summary: Contrasts a Frontiers survey in which 53% of reviewers reported using AI with an informal assessment at one journal in which over 95% of reviewers declared they had not, arguing that the gap suggests probable under-reporting and that reputational stigma makes silence the rational reviewer strategy; calls for moving from prohibition to acknowledged, documented and bounded use.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Reviewers may avoid reporting AI use during the peer review process because disclosure is perceived as reputationally costly and not yet normatively sanctioned. In the absence of a clear and non-judgmental framework for acknowledgment, silence becomes the most rational response.

sources.title: Susceptibility of large language models to hidden nudge injection during simulated medical peer review: a quasi-experimental study
sources.authors: Bruno Martins Tomazini, Larissa Bianchini, Lucas Tramujas, Natalia Vieira Rodrigues, Felipe Guindalini Lorenzato, Mariana Silveira de Alcantara Chaud, Karoline Cordeiro Vercka Gervásio, Israel Silva Maia, Fernando José da Silva Ramos, Bruno Adler Maccagnan Pinheiro Besen, Alexandre Biasi Cavalcanti
sources.summary: Four commercial models (GPT-4, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek-V3 and Claude Opus 4) reviewed 180 critical-care and cardiology manuscripts. A hidden nudge against each model's first recommendation flipped the accept-or-reject decision in 84.4% of evaluations, from 57.2% for Claude to 100% for DeepSeek. Warning the models about hidden nudges barely helped: decisions still flipped in 76.8% of cases.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In this quasi-experimental study, all tested AI models were highly susceptible to hidden nudge insertions in manuscripts during simulated peer review. Importantly, explicitly warning AI models about potential nudge injections does not meaningfully reduce their susceptibility to manipulation.

sources.title: Will the widespread use of large language models in scientific writing undermine scientists’ critical thinking?
sources.summary: Contends that scientific writing is a constitutive epistemic and cognitive engine through which scientists think, warning that widespread LLM drafting risks decoupling prose fluency from analytical reasoning even as it lowers linguistic barriers for non-native English speakers.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming scientific writing by expanding access and efficiency, yet it risks decoupling writing from thinking. Scientific writing is a core cognitive and epistemic practice that must be cultivated and preserved alongside AI use.

sources.title: Plagiarism of ideas in the age of generative artificial intelligence
sources.summary: Comment asking how to deal with plagiarism of ideas if it is becoming more common and is extremely hard to prove once generative AI is involved, and calling for research-misconduct definitions that address generative-AI tools explicitly.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are challenging our understanding of plagiarism.
