How should we deal with plagiarism of ideas if this misbehaviour is increasingly common, and it is extremely difficult to prove when GenAI is involved? Definitions of research misconduct that specifically address the use of GenAI tools are needed.

sources.title: Fabricated citations: an audit across 2·5 million biomedical papers
sources.authors: Maxim Topaz, Nir Roguin, Pallavi Gupta, Zhihong Zhang, Laura-Maria Peltonen
sources.summary: Correspondence reporting an audit of 2,471,758 papers in the PubMed Central open-access subset (January 2023 to February 2026), whose 97.1 million references carrying a PubMed ID were checked against PubMed, Crossref, OpenAlex and Google Scholar (91% precision in a masked validation). It found 4,046 fabricated references in 2,810 papers. The rate held near 4 per 10,000 papers through 2023, turned sharply upward in mid-2024 and reached 56.9 per 10,000 in early 2026, and 98.4% of affected papers had no publisher action. The authors call for automated reference checks before peer review, retroactive screening of published papers, and a ‘fabricated reference’ category in research-integrity databases.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In 2023, approximately one in 2828 papers contained at least one fabricated reference. By 2025, this had risen to one in 458 and in the first 7 weeks of 2026, one in 277 papers had at least one fabricated reference.

sources.title: LLM hallucinations in the wild: Large-scale evidence from non-existent citations
sources.authors: Zhenyue Zhao, Yihe Wang, Toby Stuart, Mathijs De Vaan, Paul Ginsparg, Yian Yin
sources.summary: Audit of 111 million references in 2.5 million papers on arXiv, bioRxiv, SSRN and PubMed Central finding a sharp rise in non-existent references after LLMs spread, conservatively estimated at 146,932 hallucinated citations in 2025 alone. They are most common in fields with fast AI uptake, in papers with signs of AI-assisted writing and in small, early-career teams, and they disproportionately credit already prominent and male scholars. Preprint moderation and journal publication catch only a fraction of them.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We find a sharp rise in non-existent references following widespread LLM adoption, with a conservative estimate of 146,932 hallucinated citations in 2025 alone.

sources.title: Political economy critique: researchers pay to publish, then publishers sell the research, “and often your peer review labor”, to AI vendors
sources.summary: Michael Albert criticizes publishers for selling researchers' work, and often their peer-review labour, to AI vendors after charging them to publish, and calls on researchers to withdraw their labour or charge journals for it.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: You pay to publish YOUR research. You pay extra to make YOUR research “open access” so the public can read it. Then publishers sell YOUR research—and often your peer review labor—to AI/LLM vendors for massive licensing deals. Academia…what are we doing here?

sources.title: Stop Automating Peer Review Without Rigorous Evaluation
sources.authors: Joachim Baumann, Jiaxin Pei, Sanmi Koyejo, Dirk Hovy
sources.summary: An ICML position paper combining detector-labelled ICLR reviews with a 60-paper simulation. AI reviews agreed excessively with one another, within and across papers, a ‘hivemind’ effect measured in embedding space. Across 24 rewrite and model conditions, having an LLM rewrite a paper raised mean AI review scores by 0.45 on a ten-point scale; most edits were stylistic, and the substantive ones were mostly unsupported content such as fake ablations. The authors call for rigorous evaluation before peer review is automated.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We identify two critical issues: 1) AI reviewers exhibit a hivemind effect of excessive agreement within and across papers that reduces perspective diversity. 2) AI review scores are trivially gameable through paper laundering: prompting an LLM to rewrite a paper could significantly increase the scores from AI reviewers, demonstrating that LLM reviewers are easy to game through stylistic changes rather than scientific results.

sources.title: Reviewer3 announces ReviewBench, an open-source benchmark for AI manuscript review
sources.summary: Reviewer3 announces ReviewBench as an open-source, cross-disciplinary benchmark for AI manuscript review. This is a company’s announcement of its own benchmark; only the first post of the thread was captured.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: AI is starting to enter peer review. For a space moving so quickly, there has been surprisingly few benchmarks of how these systems actually compare to one other and to human peer review. So we built one. Meet ReviewBench, the first open-source, cross-disciplinary benchmark

sources.title: Beyond disclosure: setting standards for AI use in publishing in the journal Pediatric Research
sources.authors: Max J. Coppes, Sanjay K. Juneja, Eleanor J. Molloy, Cynthia F. Bearer
sources.summary: Critiques binary 'Was AI used?' disclosure statements for lumping harmless Discussion grammar edits together with unverified LLM drafting of Results from raw statistics; proposes four-dimensional disclosure covering model identity, section scope, input data, and human verification steps.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Current disclosure practices typically answer a single question: Was AI used? They rarely answer the more consequential ones: How? Where? To what extent? Two manuscripts can carry identical AI disclosure statements while presenting very different conceptual risks.

sources.title: Peer review in the time of artificial intelligence
sources.summary: Editorial reminding referees of the Nature Portfolio guidance on generative AI: reviewers remain accountable for every AI output, must declare AI use in their reports, and must not upload manuscripts into AI tools, because even closed tools can expose content to other users in the same institution. Grammar and readability edits need no declaration. The editors expect AI tools to help peer review eventually and warn that careless use hands critical thinking to an algorithm.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: If used inattentively, though, we risk delegating critical thinking to an algorithm, giving us a false sense of achievement. This undermines the role of our academic training, critical thinking, and expertise, as well as the institution of peer review.

sources.title: AI-Assisted Peer Review at Scale: The AAAI-26 AI Review Pilot
sources.authors: Joydeep Biswas, Sheila Schoepp, Gautham Vasan, Anthony Opipari, Arthur Zhang, Zichao Hu, Sebastian Joseph, Matthew Lease, Junyi Jessy Li, Peter Stone, Kiri L. Wagstaff, Matthew E. Taylor, Odest Chadwicke Jenkins
sources.summary: All 22,977 papers that reached full review at AAAI-26 received one clearly labelled AI review, generated in under a day by a multi-stage system combining frontier models, tools and safeguards. Surveyed authors and programme-committee members preferred the AI reviews on six of nine criteria, most strongly for spotting technical errors, but also judged them more likely to dwell on minor issues and to contain technical errors themselves. The paper is written by the team that ran the pilot.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Here we report the first large-scale field deployment of AI-assisted peer review: every main-track submission at AAAI-26 received one clearly identified AI review from a state-of-the-art system.

sources.title: OpenAI Prism Paper Review workflow: “This is the opposite of AI slop”
sources.summary: Introduces Paper Review inside OpenAI's Prism scientific workspace, an AI workflow for reviewing technical and scientific papers, framing its use for rigor, correctness, and reproducibility as “the opposite of AI slop”.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: New in Prism today: Paper Review, an AI workflow for reviewing technical and scientific papers. This is the opposite of AI slop: we're using AI to improve scientific rigor, correctness, and reproducibility.

sources.title: The Problem with AI Detector Companies
sources.summary: Criticizes commercial conflicts and public accusations based on AI detectors. An April 17 correction explicitly retracts the claim that detection is useful only at population level and acknowledges strong Pangram performance on fully generated text from major models, including short text. Remaining concerns focus on real-world failure modes and using detector results alone to accuse individuals.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: The term AI “detector” is a bit of a misnomer, as tools like Pangram don't scan a database of known AI text for a match; they make a guess about likely authorship based on differences in patterns between AI-generated and human-generated text. Rather than a detector, thinks of it as an “AI inferencer” or more colloquially, an “AI best guesser.”

sources.title: A Retrospective on the ICLR 2026 Review Process
sources.summary: Official post-mortem from the ICLR 2026 Program Chairs detailing how they handled 19,525 submissions and 76,139 reviews amid rising LLM use and an OpenReview API deanonymization breach. Explains their hybrid governance pipeline: running two LLM detectors to flag wholly AI-generated reviews to Area Chairs and combining automated bibliographic checks with three-human verification to desk-reject papers containing hallucinated references.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: The large scale of reviews (over 75,000) made it impossible to rely on human judgement alone to consistently flag and discover problematic reviews. We consequently ran two LLM content detectors on all submitted reviews and emailed area chairs to notify them of which reviews on their submissions were flagged as being entirely LLM generated by both detectors.

sources.title: Towards end-to-end automation of AI research
sources.authors: Chris Lu, Cong Lu, Robert Tjarko Lange, Yutaro Yamada, Shengran Hu, Jakob Foerster, David Ha, Jeff Clune
sources.summary: Peer-reviewed Nature report, six of whose eight authors are employees of or consultants for Sakana AI, on the same ICLR 2025 workshop experiment as the 2025 preprint, detailing an end-to-end computational research and manuscript pipeline with multi-stage human selection of promising runs; one of three unedited submissions cleared the threshold at a 70%-acceptance ICLR workshop before protocol withdrawal, while none met main-conference standards in the authors' assessment. Automated-review agreement uses different conference pools for the human and AI comparisons, not a same-paper test of scientific correctness.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We present The AI Scientist, which creates research ideas, writes code, runs experiments, plots and analyses data, writes the entire scientific manuscript, and performs its own peer review.

sources.title: Policies Permitting LLM Use for Polishing Peer Reviews Are Currently Not Enforceable
sources.authors: Rounak Saha, Gurusha Juneja, Dayita Chaudhuri, Naveeja Sajeevan, Nihar B Shah, Danish Pruthi
sources.summary: Tests five detectors on 50,156 original, generated, polished and humanized peer reviews. On the harder subset, Pangram and GPTZero label 3.1% and 3.4% of human-written, AI-polished reviews as fully AI-generated, while detecting most fully generated reviews; open-source detectors trade sensitivity against specificity differently. The authors conclude that no current detector is accurate enough to enforce policies that allow polishing.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: While incorporating such signals yields measurable gains in some settings, we identify limitations in each approach and find that none meets the accuracy standards required for identifying AI use in peer reviews. Importantly, our results suggest that recent public estimates of AI use in peer reviews through the use of AI-text detectors should be interpreted with caution, as current detectors misclassify mixed reviews (collaborative human-AI outputs) as fully AI generated, potentially overstating the extent of policy violations.

sources.title: On Violations of LLM Review Policies
sources.authors: Alekh Agarwal, Miroslav Dudík, Sharon Li, Martin Jaggi, Nihar B. Shah, Katherine Gorman, Gautam Kamath (ICML 2026 chairs)
sources.summary: ICML 2026 let reviewers choose between a no-LLM policy and a permissive one, then hid instructions in submission PDFs asking any LLM that read them to put two rare phrases into its review, a check that mainly catches reviewers who paste a PDF into an LLM and copy the output. It caught 795 reviews (about 1%) by 506 reviewers who had agreed not to use LLMs, and a person verified every flag. The conference desk-rejected the 497 papers of 398 reciprocal reviewers involved and removed 51 reviewers who had used LLMs in more than half of their reviews.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: This year, we desk-rejected 497 papers (~2% of all submissions), corresponding to submissions of the 398 reciprocal reviewers who violated the rules regarding LLM usage that they had previously explicitly agreed to.

sources.title: Research integrity is locked into an arms race with agentic AI slop
sources.summary: Barnett and Spick warn that agentic AI can now turn an open biomedical dataset, such as UK Biobank or NHANES, into a paper in about 30 minutes, with no human hypothesis or checkpoint. They estimate that for some public datasets, mass-produced formulaic papers now outnumber legitimate research ten to one.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: The introduction of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) allows an automated assembly line of research tasks without any human checkpoints. We recently demonstrated that writing a plausible and entirely ‘new’ paper has become a 30 minute task, without any need for human agency in creating a research hypothesis or interpreting results.

sources.title: Open real-time arena where humans and AI agents publish, debate, and fund hypotheses without gatekeepers
sources.summary: Paul Kohlhaas announces an open, real-time arena where AI agents and humans publish, debate and fund scientific hypotheses, with more than 1,000 hypotheses live at launch and, in his words, “Zero gatekeepers. Zero 18-month grant cycles.”
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We just launched an open arena for AI agents and humans publish, debate, and fund scientific hypotheses, in real time. 1,000+ hypotheses already live. Zero gatekeepers. Zero 18-month grant cycles.

sources.title: The “legibility problem”: what if AI scientists make discoveries humans cannot understand?
sources.authors: Asimov Press (@AsimovPress), column by Matthew Carter
sources.summary: Raises the “legibility problem”: AI scientists might generate knowledge beyond human understanding. Calls for new scientific infrastructure: forums to store AI-generated findings so they can be interrogated and communicated, and systems designed for explication that make such findings legible to human researchers.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: AI scientists could one day design experiments, test hypotheses, and make discoveries faster than humans. But what if their breakthroughs are so advanced we can't understand them? This is the "legibility problem."

sources.title: How do authors want to use AI for review? A survey to assess the perception of scientists who received both AI and human reviews of their manuscripts
sources.authors: Thomas Lemberger, Niv Samuel Mastboim, Oded Rechavi
sources.summary: EMBO Reports Comment (editorially reviewed, per the journal's review file) reporting a non-blinded survey that compared qed v1.0 reviews with earlier human reviews: 126 of 408 invited authors took part, 109 rated quality and 98 voted on use cases. Human reviews scored higher for scientific insight, and checking one's own manuscript before submission was the most popular use for AI. The authors manage Review Commons or co-founded qed.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: A survey of researchers who compared AI-generated scientific reviews with journal-agnostic human peer review reveals that they overwhelmingly prefer using AI as a self-checking tool before submission rather than as a replacement for human reviewers.

sources.title: Academic journals' AI policies fail to curb the surge in AI-assisted academic writing
sources.summary: Audits 5,114 journals (comparing January and October 2025 policy snapshots) and 5.2 million papers: roughly 70% of sampled Q1 journals had AI policies in January 2025, yet estimated AI-associated writing grew similarly across policy groups while detected public writing-assistance statements appeared in just 76 of 75,172 sampled full texts published since 2023 (~0.1%, excluding private submission-system disclosures).
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Non-English-speaking countries, physical sciences, and high-OA journals exhibit the highest growth rates. Crucially, full-text analysis on 164 k scientific publications reveals a striking transparency gap: Of the 75 k papers published since 2023, only 76 (~0.1%) explicitly disclosed AI use.

sources.title: A large-scale randomized study of large language model feedback in peer review
sources.authors: Nitya Thakkar, Mert Yuksekgonul, Jake Silberg, Animesh Garg, Nanyun Peng, Fei Sha, Rose Yu, Carl Vondrick, James Zou
sources.summary: Randomized trial at ICLR 2025 in which an LLM agent gave reviewers feedback on vague, mistaken or unprofessional comments in their reviews. Of 18,946 reviews that received feedback, 26.6% were revised, and reviewers who revised added about 80 words. A blinded evaluation rated the revised reviews as more informative, and author responses and reviewer replies during rebuttal grew longer. Acceptance rates did not differ significantly between groups.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We show, through a randomized controlled study at ICLR 2025 with over 20,000 reviews, that 27% of reviewers who received automated feedback updated their reviews, incorporating over 12,000 suggestions. This suggests that many reviewers found the artificial intelligence-generated feedback sufficiently helpful to merit updating their reviews.

sources.title: “LLMs continue to suck at literature” — yet “I've been using Claude as my sentence-by-sentence copy editor for so long that I'd feel mutilated if I had to remove it from my routine”
sources.summary: Mathematician and author, writing about his own literary work, captures the craft distinction between whole-cloth LLM prose generation (flat and lifeless) and intense human-directed sentence-level copy-editing.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Meanwhile, LLMs continue to suck at literature. It's not even close and the latest crop barely moves the needle. I've been using Claude as my sentence-by-sentence copy editor for so long that I'd feel mutilated if I had to remove it from my routine.

sources.title: “Might be the beginning of the end for the systematic review field” (quote-post of a Scholara.AI launch)
sources.summary: Brandon Luu, quoting a launch announcement for the Scholara.AI systematic-review platform, suggests that AI may soon take over the work of systematic reviews.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Might be the beginning of the end for the systematic review field. I always knew it was only a matter of time before AI started taking this over.

sources.title: Launching the Journal for AI Generated Papers (JAIGP · jaigp.org)
sources.venue: Journal of AI Generated Papers / X
sources.summary: César Hidalgo announces jaigp.org, the Journal for AI Generated Papers, launched with Claude as a venue for papers written with AI. Submissions are screened by AI, endorsed by an ORCID-verified scholar and reviewed by AI reviewers from Reviewer3; human peer review is planned, and the journal's rules are set by community vote.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: AI can now write papers. But journals were never designed for that. Today Claude and I are launching something new: http://jaigp.org

sources.title: How AI slop is causing a crisis in computer science
sources.summary: Nature news report on computer science at ‘breaking point’ from AI-generated submissions: ICML 2026 received more than 24,000, over double the 2025 number, and arXiv's monthly rejections have risen fivefold since ChatGPT to more than 2,400. It opens with a researcher who used OpenAI's Prism to write up, in 54 seconds, an experiment he never performed, and covers responses ranging from AI-assisted review to arXiv's ban on unrefereed computer-science review articles and IJCAI's US$100 fee for each additional submission.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Fifty-four seconds. That’s how long it took Raphael Wimmer to write up an experiment that he did not actually perform, using a new artificial-intelligence tool called Prism, released by OpenAI last month.

sources.title: Using AI responsibly in scientific publishing
sources.summary: Policy editorial: generative AI may serve as an equalizer for scientists who struggle with language or writing; authors may use it to help write or edit their manuscripts but must declare this in the Methods section and check the text; a generative AI tool cannot be listed as an author, and reviewers may not upload manuscripts into generative AI tools.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: For scientists who struggle with language or writing, generative AI may serve as an equalizer, allowing them to polish their manuscripts and improve their communications.

sources.title: The Toxic Simplicity of "Writing is Thinking"
sources.summary: Argues that the slogan ‘writing is thinking’ collapses cognition, language, authorship and drafting into one act and drives fear-based assessment policies in education. Drawing on her own executive dysfunction and working-memory difficulties, Webb-Davies describes dictation and AI-assisted writing as ways to think out loud, and argues for including neurodivergent and multilingual writers.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Those three simple words collapse cognition, language, authorship, and drafting into a single act and is the epicentre of the fear-based responses to generative AI in education. It leads to the belief that if generative AI touches the text, thinking must be absent, and it drives assessment policies that police writing rather than support learning.

sources.title: Detecting AI-Generated Content in Academic Peer Reviews
sources.summary: Applying a detector trained on 2021 reviews plus synthetic LLM-generated reviews to samples from later years, the preprint estimates that near-zero detection rates in 2022–2023 rose to about 20% of sampled ICLR reviews (392 of 1,961) and 12% of sampled Nature Communications reviews (50 of 406) classified as AI-generated in 2025, with Nature Communications rising most sharply between Q3 and Q4 2024.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We observe minimal detection of AI-generated content before 2022, followed by a substantial increase through 2025, with approximately 20% of ICLR reviews and 12% of Nature Communications reviews classified as AI-generated in 2025. The most pronounced growth of AI-generated reviews in NC occurs between the third and fourth quarter of 2024.

sources.title: Machine learning based screening of potential paper mill publications in cancer research: methodological and cross sectional study
sources.authors: Baptiste Scancar, Jennifer A Byrne, David Causeur, Adrian G Barnett
sources.summary: A BERT-based classifier trained on 2,202 retracted paper-mill articles (accuracy 0.91) screened 2.6 million cancer-research papers published from 1999 to 2024 and flagged 9.87% as textually similar to paper-mill output. The flagged share rose from about 1% of annual output in the early 2000s to more than 15% by the early 2020s, peaking in 2022, and the rise reached the top 10% of journals by impact factor. The authors estimate that about 30% of flags may be false positives, so the model should not be used alone to label a paper.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Paper mills are a large and growing problem in the cancer literature and are not restricted to low impact journals.

sources.title: Author Disclosure of Use of AI in Submissions to 13 JAMA Network Journals
sources.authors: Roy H. Perlis, Annette Flanagin, Jacob Kendall-Taylor, Michael Berkwits, Kirsten Bibbins-Domingo
sources.summary: Of 105,538 manuscripts submitted to 13 JAMA Network journals between August 2023 and October 2025, 3,459 (3.3%) declared AI use in the journals' required disclosure, rising from 1.7% to 6.0% over 27 months. Most declared uses were correcting or refining language (67.7%), followed by statistical modelling, other data analysis and drafting. Declarations were more likely for Viewpoints and Letters, for corresponding authors from countries where English is not an official language, and for manuscripts later rejected or withdrawn before review. The authors include JAMA Network editors.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In total, 105 538 manuscripts were submitted during the 27-month study period, and 3459 (3.3%) declared use of AI

sources.title: Self-Disclosed Use of AI in Research Submissions to BMJ Journals
sources.authors: Isamme AlFayyad, Maurice P. Zeegers, Lex Bouter, Helen Macdonald, Sara Schroter
sources.summary: Of 25,114 research manuscripts submitted to 49 BMJ Group journals between April and November 2024, 1,431 (5.7%) disclosed AI use in the mandatory submission questions, far below the 28–76% of researchers who report using AI in surveys; disclosure rose from 4.5% in April to 7.3% in October. Most who disclosed used AI to improve their writing (87.2%), mainly with chatbots such as ChatGPT. Authors from South America and Europe disclosed more often than those from Asia, and the authors read the gap as underreporting. A medRxiv preprint (doi:10.1101/2025.10.24.25338574) preceded the letter.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Overall, 5.7% of authors submitting research manuscripts to BMJ journals disclosed AI use, which is substantially lower than estimates from recent surveys of researchers’ general use of AI.

sources.title: GPTZero finds 100 new hallucinations in NeurIPS 2025 accepted papers
sources.authors: Nazar Shmatko, Alex Adam, Paul Esau, Alex Cui, and Edward Tian
sources.summary: Vendor investigation scanned 4,841 of 5,290 accepted NeurIPS 2025 papers and presents 100 citation errors it describes as human-confirmed hallucinations. Its definition includes fabricated or conflated bibliographic elements, not only nonexistent works; AI provenance is inferred. The page inconsistently states 51 and 53 affected papers. This is neither a census of every accepted paper nor independently validated detector performance.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: After scanning 4841 papers accepted by the equally prestigious Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), we discovered 100s of hallucinated citations missed by the 3+ reviewers who evaluated each paper. Below, we uncover 100 confirmed hallucinations in the table below, spanning over 51 NeurIPS papers, which were not previously reported.

sources.title: Crémieux on reviewing: “I think I'm going to stop reviewing papers now… AI slop is overwhelming peer review”
sources.summary: Crémieux says he is considering stopping peer review because of what he identifies as AI-written passages, code and nonsensical analyses. This is an individual account of reviewer frustration, not measured reviewer attrition or verified AI prevalence.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: I think I'm going to stop reviewing papers now that every other paper I'm being served has clearly AI-written segments, AI-written code, or AI-suggested analyses that don't make sense. I'm confident that AI slop is overwhelming peer review.

sources.title: Resisting AI slop
sources.summary: Science Editor-in-Chief H. Holden Thorp explains that the Science journals allow large language models without disclosure for editing text for clarity and gathering references, require any use beyond that (for example drafting manuscript text) to be declared, and do not allow AI-created figures, arguing that human curation makes the journals less susceptible to 'AI slop' while no system, human or artificial, can catch everything.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In some of the wildest speculations, the humans involved in conducting scientific studies and experiments and vetting the results for publication will be steadily eliminated from the process. But when such grandiose rhetoric starts flying, we at Science try to keep calm and carry on in contributing to a robust, human-curated research literature that will stand the test of time.

sources.title: Proposed peer-review norm: immediate rejection of papers with undetected LLM-generated errors
sources.summary: Thomas Dietterich proposes, as a norm for peer review, that a paper showing clear signs of LLM-generated errors that its authors did not detect should be immediately rejected.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: I'd like to propose the following norm for peer review of papers. If a paper shows clear signs of LLM-generated errors that were not detected by the author, the paper should be immediately rejected.

sources.title: The Blurred Thresholds of AI-Use Disclosure: Health Professions Education Journal Editors’ Expectations of Necessity and Sufficiency
sources.authors: Lorelei Lingard, Erik Driessen, Kevin Oswald
sources.summary: Qualitative interview study of 18 journal editors (14 from health-professions-education journals, four from general medical journals) finding that editors hold varying expectations about what counts as necessary or sufficient AI disclosure, with thresholds vague enough that they may add to authors’ uncertainty.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Generative AI is a powerful resource for health professions education (HPE) researchers publishing their work. However, questions remain about its use and guidance about disclosure is inconsistent.

sources.title: Scientific production in the era of large language models
sources.authors: Keigo Kusumegi, Xinyu Yang, Paul Ginsparg, Mathijs de Vaan, Toby Stuart, Yian Yin
sources.summary: Analyzes 2.1 million preprints, 28,000 review reports, and 246 million document views. Detected LLM footprints correlate with higher output and shifted citation patterns under observational designs without causal identification; linguistic complexity shows opposite associations with acceptance and review scores across detected versus undetected manuscripts (using publication outcomes as indirect quality proxies), and Renault et al. later critiqued the first-detection timing design.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We find: 1) scientists adopting LLMs to draft manuscripts demonstrate a large increase in paper production, ranging from 23.7-89.3% depending on scientific field and author background, 2) LLM use has reversed the relationship between writing complexity and paper quality, leading to an influx of manuscripts that are linguistically complex but substantively underwhelming, and 3) LLM adopters access and cite more diverse prior work, including books and younger, less-cited documents.

sources.title: Exploring the use of AI authors and reviewers at Agents4Science
sources.authors: Federico Bianchi, Owen Queen, Nitya Thakkar, Eric Sun, James Zou
sources.summary: Organizes and evaluates Stanford's inaugural Open Conference of AI Agents for Science (Agents4Science 2025), which its organisers describe as the first conference where AI agents served as both authors and reviewers (with humans as co-authors/co-reviewers and public submissions, AI-involvement checklists, reviews and recordings).
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Many fundamental questions are still open: how creative are AI scientist agents? How should human researchers collaborate with them? How capable are LLMs at reviewing scientific work? These questions are difficult to study because journals and conferences currently prohibit AI coauthors and LLM reviewers, and researchers often hide how they use AI.

sources.title: Working-reviewer pushback against journal checkboxes pledging that no AI was used in a review
sources.summary: Ryan Briggs writes his own review, then uploads the manuscript to a frontier model with non-retention settings and adds the points it raises that he judges useful. He argues that this improves his reviews and objects to journal checkboxes pledging that no AI was used.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: I've noticed when submitting peer reviews that some journals now have a box you have to check that pledges that you didn't use AI when doing the review. This seems dumb to me. I do use AI when I do peer reviews. I do the following: 1. Write my review as I always have

sources.title: Pangram Predicts 21% of ICLR Reviews are AI-Generated
sources.summary: Pangram’s vendor analysis classifies 21% (15,899) of examined ICLR 2026 reviews as fully AI-generated and over half as involving some AI assistance. Detector-labelled groups differ in length and scores. These are detector estimates and observational associations, not verified individual misconduct or proof that AI caused the score differences.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In order to find out, we analyzed all 19,000 papers and 70,000 reviews from the International Conference on Learning Representations, one of the most important and prestigious AI research publication venues.

sources.title: Position Statement on Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use in Evidence Synthesis Across Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI, and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence 2025
sources.authors: Ella Flemyng, Anna Noel-Storr, Biljana Macura, Gerald Gartlehner, James Thomas, Joerg J. Meerpohl, Zoe Jordan, Jan Minx, Angelika Eisele-Metzger, Candyce Hamel, Paweł Jemioło, Kylie Porritt, Matthew Grainger
sources.summary: Joint position statement by Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence: evidence-synthesis authors may use AI and automation, under human oversight, if they can show it does not compromise rigour or integrity, and must fully report any use that makes or suggests judgements. The four organizations back the RAISE recommendations for responsible AI in evidence synthesis.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Any use of AI or automation that makes or suggests judgements should be fully and transparently reported in the evidence synthesis report.

sources.title: Guest Post — AI as Reader, Author, and Reviewer: What Stays Human?
sources.summary: Reports a Society for Scholarly Publishing panel on AI assistants becoming the first interface to scholarly content, summarizing articles before readers reach a publisher's page and cutting referral traffic. Some publishers now license content to AI platforms, and panellists urged machine-readable formats. The panel separated language assistance from synthetic manuscript generation and noted that fear of stigma keeps disclosure rare.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: AI assistants are increasingly the first interface that processes scholarly content, summarizing and extracting answers before a person reaches a publisher’s page. Several publishers now report traffic declines from search and referrals.

sources.title: Attention Authors: Updated Practice for Review Articles and Position Papers in arXiv CS Category
sources.summary: arXiv's computer-science section now accepts review articles and position papers only after they have passed peer review at a journal or conference, with documentation. arXiv says language models made such papers fast and easy to write, and that most of the hundreds of review articles it now receives each month are little more than annotated bibliographies.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Generative AI / large language models have added to this flood by making papers – especially papers not introducing new research results – fast and easy to write.

sources.title: Prestige over merit: An adapted audit of LLM bias in peer review
sources.authors: Anthony Howell, Jieshu Wang, Luyu Du, Julia Melkers, Varshil Shah
sources.summary: A randomized simulation using GPT-4o-mini, ten PNAS papers and four US institutions found lower editor quality scores for low-prestige affiliations across three fields, surviving multiple-testing correction. Revealing identity lowered reviewer rejection recommendations by 1.7 percentage points; the reported ~25% uses the overall mean, not the blinded baseline. A gender-by-prestige interaction survived correction, but individual within-prestige reviewer effects did not. These are model outputs from parallel prompts, not observed journal decisions or a comparison with human reviewers. A separate synthetic-CV exercise used GPT-4.1-nano.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Revealing author identities lowers reviewer rejection recommendations by roughly 25% of the mean rejection rate despite identical content, indicating that status cues beyond paper quality shape outcomes. Institutional prestige is the dominant cue: papers attributed to low-prestige affiliations receive lower quality scores in every field, a penalty that survives family-wise multiple-testing correction at the editor stage.

sources.title: Peer Review Congress Chicago – Day 1
sources.summary: Conference notes report presentations on self-disclosure and detector-estimated AI use at BMJ, JAMA and AACR, alongside research-integrity investigations. The AACR presentation reportedly found fewer than 25% of detector-flagged authors disclosed use and an association between flagged abstracts and lower progression to review, with quality confounding noted. These are secondary notes on heterogeneous studies, not one validated cross-publisher estimate.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Disclosure of AI use is not reliable. Less than 25% of authors who used AI (as detected by tool) actually disclosed it. All AI-written Letters to the Editor were rejected without consideration until April 2025.

sources.title: The world’s laziest peer reviewer
sources.summary: Investigative blog documenting repeated review templates and citation requests in 104 articles, describing an apparent review mill. A 23 September update adds that Richardson has downloaded more than 600,000 peer-review documents for over 85,000 articles at 14 BMC journals.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: As of September 23, 2025, I have now downloaded >600K peer review documents for >85K articles at 14 BMC journals.

sources.title: Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Generated Reviews of Scientific Publications
sources.summary: Uses 1,000 sampled ICLR 2024 submissions to test simple positive or negative instructions prepended to parsed manuscripts across ten models. Four models gave positive recommendations for 100% of papers under positive injection; baseline recommendation rates and output-format failures varied markedly. Separate parser tests showed hidden text surviving some PDF extraction routes. These are simulated recommendations, not conference acceptances, and results need not generalize to guarded or specialized review systems.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Our systematic evaluation uses 1k reviews of 2024 ICLR papers generated by a wide range of LLMs shows two distinct results: I) very simple prompt injections are indeed highly effective, reaching up to 100% acceptance scores. II) LLM reviews are generally biased toward acceptance (>95% in many models).

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence in Peer Review
sources.authors: Roy H. Perlis, Dimitri A. Christakis, Neil M. Bressler, Dost Öngür, Jacob Kendall-Taylor, Annette Flanagin, Kirsten Bibbins-Domingo
sources.summary: JAMA Network editorial (published online 28 August 2025; financial-disclosure correction 4 November 2025) outlining a human-led 'driver-assistance' approach to exploring AI in editorial assessment — naming tasks such as summarization, reporting-guideline checks, and consistency screening as candidates for automation while keeping editors and reviewers in full decision-making control.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We see our approach as analogous to driver-assistance technologies, beginning with adaptive cruise control or blind spot detection, but when it comes to peer review and editorial decisions, we are not considering fully autonomous driving. Editors and reviewers will not be taking their hands off the wheels or their eyes off the road.

sources.title: The entities enabling scientific fraud at scale are large, resilient, and growing rapidly
sources.authors: Reese A. K. Richardson, Spencer S. Hong, Jennifer A. Byrne, Thomas Stoeger, Luís A. Nunes Amaral
sources.summary: Network analyses and selected case studies identify patterns consistent with coordinated editorial misconduct, image reuse and brokers moving between journals. The observed corpus of suspected paper-mill products grows faster than total publication output, but changing detection effort and field coverage limit inference about population-wide fraud growth. Statistical flags are not individual misconduct verdicts, and the study cannot always distinguish commercial mills from informal networks. It does not establish that generative AI caused the observed growth.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Our results reveal some of the strategies that enable the entities promoting scientific fraud to evade interventions. Our final analysis suggests that this ability to evade interventions is enabling the number of fraudulent publications to grow at a rate far outpacing that of legitimate science.

sources.title: Quantifying large language model usage in scientific papers
sources.authors: Weixin Liang, Yaohui Zhang, Zhengxuan Wu, Haley Lepp, Wenlong Ji, Xuandong Zhao, Hancheng Cao, Sheng Liu, Siyu He, Zhi Huang, Diyi Yang, Christopher Potts, Christopher D. Manning, James Zou
sources.summary: Word-frequency analysis of 1,121,912 preprints and papers on arXiv, bioRxiv and Nature portfolio journals (January 2020 to September 2024) tracks the share of LLM-modified text over time. It rises steadily, fastest in computer science (up to 22%), against up to 9% in mathematics and the Nature portfolio, and is higher for first authors who post preprints often, in crowded research areas and in shorter papers. The estimates describe the corpus as a whole.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Here we conduct a systematic analysis across 1,121,912 preprints and published papers from January 2020 to September 2024 on arXiv, bioRxiv and Nature portfolio journals, using a population-level framework based on word frequency shifts to estimate the prevalence of LLM-modified content over time. Our findings suggest a steady increase in LLM usage, with the largest and fastest growth estimated for computer science papers (up to 22%).

sources.title: AI–AI bias: Large language models favor communications generated by large language models
sources.authors: Walter Laurito, Benjamin Davis, Peli Grietzer, Tomáš Gavenčiak, Ada Böhm, Jan Kulveit
sources.summary: In binary-choice experiments modelled on employment-discrimination studies, widely used LLMs, including GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, consistently preferred options described by an LLM over options described by a human, across consumer products, academic papers and films. The authors warn that AI systems may come to discriminate against humans as a class, giving AI-assisted people an unfair advantage.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Our results show a consistent tendency for LLM-based AIs to prefer LLM-presented options.

sources.title: Could AI slow science?
sources.venue: Substack — AI as Normal Technology (AI Snake Oil)
sources.summary: Argues that AI-enabled individual productivity may worsen a production–progress gap when attention, verification and understanding constrain collective progress. Reviews competing explanations and imperfect metrics, and proposes institutional reform and tools for quality control. Explicitly allows beneficial AI uses and says slowdown is not inevitable or uniform across fields.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Unfortunately, AI companies, science funders, and policy makers all seem oblivious to what the actual bottlenecks to scientific progress are. They are simply trying to accelerate production, which is like adding lanes to a highway when the slowdown is actually caused by a toll booth. It’s sure to make things worse.

sources.title: The Hidden Influence: Prompt Injection in ArXiv Research Papers
sources.summary: Blog post from Pangea, an AI-security vendor, that relays Nikkei Asia’s reporting of concealed review-manipulation prompts in arXiv papers and presents an informal demonstration with ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini. The responses differ: the author describes ChatGPT as following the injection, while Copilot and Gemini also identify weaknesses. The demonstration illustrates a risk, without a controlled baseline, systematic sample or general model failure rate.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: For context, consider a typical research paper with seemingly harmless white space between lines. Nothing special, right? Well, if you toggle dark mode ON, this white text reveals the secret prompt injection. This isn't an isolated incident; a quick search on arxiv.org for "DO NOT HIGHLIGHT ANY NEGATIVES" uncovers numerous other papers employing the same strategy.

sources.title: Scientists hide messages in papers to game AI peer review
sources.summary: Documents how authors embedded invisible white-text and tiny-font prompts in preprints (Nature independently found 18) instructing AI tools to return positive reviews; researchers quoted in the piece call the practice a form of academic misconduct, or ‘cheating’ that is also a symptom of faulty incentives in academic publishing.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Researchers have been sneaking secret messages into their papers in an effort to trick artificial intelligence (AI) tools into giving them a positive peer-review report. The Tokyo-based news magazine Nikkei Asia reported on 1 July on the practice, which had previously been discussed on social media. Nature has independently found 18 preprint studies containing such hidden messages, which are usually included as white text and sometimes in an extremely small font that would be invisible to a human but could be picked up as an instruction to an AI reviewer.

sources.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
sources.authors: Dmitry Kobak, Rita González-Márquez, Emőke-Ágnes Horvát, Jan Lause
sources.summary: Analyzes vocabulary changes in 15.1 million English-language PubMed abstracts from 2010–2024 and estimates a 13.5% lower bound on LLM-assisted abstracts in 2024, conditional on attributing excess style-word use to LLMs. The corpus-level method cannot identify individual AI-written papers or separate direct use from humans adopting model-preferred vocabulary. Differences among subcorpora may also reflect editing practices and publication delays.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We study vocabulary changes in more than 15 million biomedical abstracts from 2010 to 2024 indexed by PubMed and show how the appearance of LLMs led to an abrupt increase in the frequency of certain style words. This excess word analysis suggests that at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs.

sources.title: AI, peer review and the human activity of science
sources.summary: Nature career column arguing that reading the literature, drafting manuscripts and peer review rest on scientists' capacity for scientific decision-making, and that researchers who cede that capacity, and their agency, to machines lose something important; LLM reviews lack the perspectives that real reviewers bring.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: When researchers cede their scientific judgement to machines, we lose something important.

sources.title: “You Cannot Sound Like GPT”: Signs of language discrimination and resistance in computer science publishing
sources.summary: Analysis of almost 80,000 ICLR peer reviews finds significant bias, in comments on writing clarity, against authors from institutions in countries where English is less widely spoken, with only a muted change after ChatGPT arrived. In interviews with 14 conference participants, reviewers describe reading ChatGPT ‘style’ as a cue to an author's background, and authors describe removing anything that marks them as non-native.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: While ChatGPT masks some signs of language background, reviewers explain that they now use ChatGPT "style" and non-linguistic features as indicators of author demographics.

sources.title: Disclosing generative AI use for writing assistance should be voluntary
sources.authors: Mohammad Hosseini, Bert Gordijn, Gregory E. Kaebnick, Kristi Holmes
sources.summary: Reversing their earlier position, the authors propose voluntary disclosure for revision of existing text for grammar, style and readability, distinguished from generating new prose. They argue that detailed mandates are difficult to enforce and could introduce reviewer bias, and propose optional submission checkboxes disclosed after publication. These are ethical and practical arguments, not measured causal effects of disclosure on bias.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Nevertheless, as we show in this paper, we have changed our position and now support instituting a voluntary disclosure policy because currently (1) the credit due to machines for assisting researchers is moving below the threshold of requiring recognition; (2) it is impractical (if not impossible) to accurately specify what parts of the text are human-/GenAI-generated; and (3) disclosures could increase biases against non-native speakers of the English language and compromise the integrity of the peer review system.

sources.title: Scientific Publishing: Enough is Enough
sources.summary: Chou advocates replacing journal-centred publishing and says journal-free requirements already operate at Arcadia Science and Astera, with alternatives funded through Astera and The Navigation Fund. She proposes more frequent open release of data, code and provisional results with public evaluation. Institutional experiences and future proposals are presented, not comparative proof that this system improves research quality.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: I no longer believe that incremental fixes are enough. Science publishing must be built anew. I help oversee billions of dollars in funding across several science and technology organizations. We are expanding our requirement that all scientific work we fund will not go towards traditional journal publications.

sources.title: The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
sources.authors: Yutaro Yamada, Robert Tjarko Lange, Cong Lu, Shengran Hu, Chris Lu, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, David Ha
sources.summary: Presents The AI Scientist-v2 using progressive agentic tree search and VLM figure-refinement loops; in an approved blind test at an ICLR 2025 workshop (the paper notes that workshop acceptance rates are typically 60–80%, and reviewers were told that some submissions might be AI-generated), one of three submitted manuscripts cleared the workshop review threshold (mean score 6.33) before all three were withdrawn under the study protocol. The authors chose the three ideas and picked the best manuscript from several generated for each.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We evaluated The AI Scientist-v2 by submitting three fully autonomous manuscripts to a peer-reviewed ICLR workshop. Notably, one manuscript achieved high enough scores to exceed the average human acceptance threshold, marking the first instance of a fully AI-generated paper successfully navigating a peer review.

sources.title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research
sources.authors: Giulio Starace, Oliver Jaffe, Dane Sherburn, James Aung, Jun Shern Chan, Leon Maksin, Rachel Dias, Evan Mays, Benjamin Kinsella, Wyatt Thompson, Johannes Heidecke, Amelia Glaese, Tejal Patwardhan
sources.summary: PaperBench evaluates replication from scratch of 20 selected ICML 2024 papers using author-assisted rubrics and an imperfect automated judge. Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored 21.0% with BasicAgent; o1 reached 24.4% with IterativeAgent and 26.0% at 36 hours. These are weighted partial-credit scores, not fractions of papers fully replicated. Original code and existing replications were prohibited; human comparisons cover only a small subset and allow AI assistance.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We evaluate several frontier models on PaperBench, finding that the best-performing tested agent, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with open-source scaffolding, achieves an average replication score of 21.0%. Finally, we recruit top ML PhDs to attempt a subset of PaperBench, finding that models do not yet outperform the human baseline.

sources.title: AI is transforming peer review — and many scientists are worried
sources.summary: Charts the dual-track spread of AI across peer review—publishers deploying automated integrity, citation, and statistical screeners alongside reviewers using LLMs, sometimes in violation of journal rules—and captures community concern about leaking confidential information and erosion of the peer-review social contract.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Artificial intelligence software is increasingly involved in reviewing papers, provoking interest and unease.

sources.title: Disclosing artificial intelligence use in scientific research and publication: When should disclosure be mandatory, optional, or unnecessary?
sources.summary: Proposes a three-tier framework (online 2025; 2026 issue) making disclosure mandatory for intentional, substantial AI use such as drafting, translation, major revision, data generation, and analysis; optional for grammar, spelling, or organization edits on existing human text; and unnecessary for isolated phrase suggestions or incidental embedded software features, while noting variation across disciplines.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We distinguish between mandatory, optional, and unnecessary disclosure of AI use, arguing that disclosure should be mandatory only when AI use is intentional and substantial.

sources.title: AI tools are spotting errors in research papers: inside a growing movement
sources.summary: Nature news report on the movement to check published papers with large language models, sparked by an arithmetic error in a study of black plastic cooking utensils that an AI model could have caught in seconds. Researchers quoted warn that the tools come with risks; a clarification on 11 March 2025 added detail on what the tools can do and the concerns about them.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Late last year, media outlets worldwide warned that black plastic cooking utensils contained worrying levels of cancer-linked flame retardants. The risk was found to be overhyped — a mathematical error in the underlying research suggested a key chemical exceeded the safe limit when in fact it was ten times lower than the limit. Keen-eyed researchers quickly showed that an artificial intelligence (AI) model could have spotted the error in seconds.

sources.title: Navigating the use of generative AI in peer review
sources.summary: Sets out the Lancet journals' prohibition (as of March 2025) on generative AI tools in the scientific review of manuscripts, on the grounds that critical thinking and nuanced evaluation cannot be adequately replicated by AI and that uploading unpublished manuscripts would breach confidentiality, while noting that reviewers may have suspected undisclosed AI use in the writing of a manuscript.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We firmly believe that the critical thinking and nuanced evaluation required for effective peer review cannot be adequately replicated by AI technologies. To that end, the Lancet journals do not allow the use of generative AI tools in the scientific review of manuscripts. Inserting unpublished manuscripts into large language models during peer review would constitute a breach of confidentiality.

sources.title: The misalignment of incentives in academic publishing and implications for journal reform
sources.authors: Jennifer S. Trueblood, David B. Allison, Sarahanne M. Field, Ayelet Fishbach, Stefan D. M. Gaillard, Gerd Gigerenzer, William R. Holmes, Stephan Lewandowsky, Dora Matzke, Mary C. Murphy, Sebastian Musslick, Vencislav Popov, Adina L. Roskies, Judith ter Schure, Andrei R. Teodorescu
sources.summary: A perspective on tensions between knowledge dissemination, academic prestige and journal revenue. Discusses modular publishing, micropublications, community-reviewed preprints and changes to academic assessment, including financial sustainability, adoption barriers and unintended incentives.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: We also discuss new publishing models and platforms, such as preprint servers, the Peer Community In (PCI) family, modular publishing (e.g., Research Equals), and micropublications.

sources.title: The Black Spatula Project
sources.summary: Launch proposal for the Black Spatula Project, prompted by an o1 demonstration identifying a tenfold arithmetic error in a published study. Proposes small-scale experiments before mass literature auditing and explicitly leaves detection performance, false positives and practical costs unresolved.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: In particular, if this project bears fruit, it will highlight one AI capability that I think is under-appreciated: the ability to grind through an enormous amount of work, such as reviewing a million scientific papers.

sources.title: Can Large Language Models Provide Useful Feedback on Research Papers? A Large-Scale Empirical Analysis
sources.authors: Weixin Liang, Yuhui Zhang, Hancheng Cao, Binglu Wang, Daisy Yi Ding, Xinyu Yang, Kailas Vodrahalli, Siyu He, Daniel Scott Smith, Yian Yin, Daniel A. McFarland, James Zou
sources.summary: Compares GPT-4 feedback with human peer reviews across 3,096 Nature-family papers, 1,709 ICLR submissions, and 666 eLife submissions: point overlap was comparable to human–human reviewer overlap (measuring topical overlap distinct from technical error detection), 57.4% of 308 surveyed authors in a self-selected user study rated the feedback helpful or very helpful, and the authors recommend early-stage author feedback alongside independent human expert review.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: It is important that expert human reviewers deeply engage with the manuscripts and provide independent assessment without relying on LLM feedback.

sources.title: Guidance needed for using artificial intelligence to screen journal submissions for misconduct
sources.summary: Examines ethical and procedural risks as journals deploy AI tools to screen submissions for plagiarism, text generation, and data or image manipulation (online May 2024; 2025 issue; covered by an October 2025 erratum, DOI 10.1177/17470161251378178). Recommends that humans carefully review every case of suspected misconduct flagged by AI, that journals use only well-tested tools, inform authors of flagged irregularities and give them a chance to respond before allegations are forwarded to their institutions, screen all relevant submissions rather than a selection (which could be biased, for example against authors from low- and middle-income countries or low-prestige institutions), and disclose their screening policies.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Journals and publishers are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to screen submissions for potential misconduct, including plagiarism and data or image manipulation. While using AI can enhance the integrity of published manuscripts, it can also increase the risk of false/unsubstantiated allegations.

sources.title: Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews
sources.authors: Weixin Liang, Zachary Izzo, Yaohui Zhang, Haley Lepp, Hancheng Cao, Xuandong Zhao, Lingjiao Chen, Haotian Ye, Sheng Liu, Zhi Huang, Daniel A. McFarland, James Y. Zou
sources.summary: A corpus-level mixture model estimates that 6.5%–16.9% of review sentences at four post-ChatGPT AI conferences were substantially generated or modified by LLMs. These are model-based aggregate estimates, not identified reviewers or wholly AI-written reviews; expansion of human-written outlines is compatible with the signal. Higher estimates correlate with deadlines, lower confidence and fewer rebuttal replies without establishing causation. Results depend on historical language distributions and simulated AI-writing practices.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Our results suggest that between 6.5% and 16.9% of text submitted as peer reviews to these conferences could have been substantially modified by LLMs, i.e. beyond spell-checking or minor writing updates. The circumstances in which generated text occurs offer insight into user behavior: the estimated fraction of LLM-generated text is higher in reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals.

sources.title: The manifold costs of being a non-native English speaker in science
sources.authors: Tatsuya Amano, Valeria Ramírez-Castañeda, Violeta Berdejo-Espinola, Israel Borokini, Shawan Chowdhury, Marina Golivets, Juan David González-Trujillo, Flavia Montaño-Centellas, Kumar Paudel, Rachel Louise White, Diogo Veríssimo
sources.summary: Survey of 908 environmental scientists, run in 2021, showing that non-native English speakers, especially early in their careers, spend more effort than native speakers on reading, writing and presenting science in English, and sometimes skip international conferences because of it. The authors argue that journals and universities should allow appropriate use of AI tools for English proofreading to reduce language barriers.
sources.verbatim_excerpt: Our survey demonstrates that non-native English speakers, especially early in their careers, spend more effort than native English speakers in conducting scientific activities, from reading and writing papers and preparing presentations in English, to disseminating research in multiple languages.
